## ON THE CIRCULAR ENCLOSURE OF THE DUAL.
### 19th Seal.

A has around itself B and C; B has D and E; C has E and F; D has G and H; E has I and K; F has L and M; G has N and O; 
<margin>5</margin> H has P and Q; I has R and S; K has T and V; L has X and Z; M has a and b; N has c and d; O has e and f; P has g and h; Q has i and k; R has l and m; S has n and o; T has p and q; V has r and s; X has t and v; Z has x and z.
<note>This seal describes a branching tree structure where each letter generates two more, creating a "circular" or "encyclical" expansion of pairs—essentially a binary system—used for organizing information in memory.</note>

## ON THE COMPOSITE AND THE ELEMENT.
### 20th Seal.

<margin>10</margin> An epigram or an ode recalled to me a counted group of ten. This poem was divided into its own distinct parts: first it suggested books of sections, then chapters of books, and shortly thereafter portions of chapters. Meanwhile, the universal and general subject matter brought forth <margin>15</margin> reasoned <note>original: ratiocinativos</note> discourses, and these produced for me their own propositions and maxims. From these, what could have prevented an approach toward simple <note>or "elementary"</note> terms? Thus, "I HATE" <note>original: *ODI*</note> of the first part, "THE UNINITIATED" <note>original: *PROFANUM*</note> of the second, "RABBLE" <note>original: *VULGUS*</note> of the third, "AND I DRIVE AWAY" <note>original: *ET ARCEO*</note> of the fourth <note>Bruno is quoting the famous opening of Horace’s Odes, Book 3, Ode 1: "Odi profanum vulgus et arceo." He uses this well-known verse to demonstrate how a complex thought can be broken down into individual "elements" or keywords for memory storage.</note>, revealed...

<meta>This page transitions from the primary text of Giordano Bruno’s mnemonic systems to an editorial preface or note—likely by the 19th-century editors Felice Tocco and Francesco Fiorentino—regarding the bibliographic history and printing discrepancies of Bruno's London publications.</meta>

In the annotations placed before each of the pamphlets contained in this second part of the second volume, everything necessary for the understanding of the <term>critical apparatus</term> <note>The set of notes explaining textual variants and editorial choices</note> has been stated. It remains for us to say something about the manner in which the small London volume is composed, which contains the *Art of Remembering* <note>original: 'Ars reminiscendi'</note>, the *Thirty Seals* <note>original: 'Triginta Sigilli'</note> etc., and the *Seal of Seals* <note>original: 'Sigillus Sigillorum'</note>; but for now, we see no hypothesis that resolves every difficulty.¹ Let it suffice to note that a *Minor Explanation* <note>original: 'Explicatio minor'</note> (see p. 160, line 20) would seem to imply the existence of a *Major Explanation* <note>original: 'Explicatio maior'</note>; one might therefore believe that the pamphlet now reprinted from page 73 to page 119—a pamphlet which is missing in some copies and is, in any case, printed on different paper from the rest—is nothing but a second draft of a larger, destroyed work. But why the second draft would have been substituted in some copies and not in others, we cannot explain. On the other hand, if the pamphlet missing in some copies was printed after the rest, how can we explain that the seal *Gorgias* (p. 148) of the *Minor Explanation* erroneously becomes *Heaven* <note>original: Caelum</note> (p. 94) there, which is already the title of the second Seal in both pamphlets (p. 80 and 122)? Nor can a simple writing or printing error on page 94 be admitted, because the words "It was a figure of worldly eternity, a symbol of the circling earth" <note>original Latin: 'Erat mundanae aeternitatis figura, circumgyrantis terrae typus'</note> etc. do not seem to be of such a nature as to suggest that the title does not suit the text. Perhaps an explanation for such difficulties can be provided [by...]

---

¹ See Tocco, *The Latin Works of G. B.* [Giordano Bruno] p. 63 and following.

...satisfactory to whoever examines different copies from those we were able to see; since probably our two copies (the Braidense <note>The Braidense National Library in Milan</note> and the Guicciardiniano <note>Referring to the collection of Piero Guicciardini, now in the National Central Library of Florence</note>; cf. on p. 74) are also incomplete, as neither one contains more than eight ¹ geometric figures (pp. 109–116), while it is to be assumed that Bruno did not renounce the pleasure of graphically representing others among his thirty <term>Seals</term> <note>Mnemonic diagrams used in Bruno's complex system of memory and philosophy</note>.

The *One Hundred and Twenty Articles* <note>original: 'Centum et viginti articuli'</note> etc. are certainly not in their proper place in this volume, except by chronological order; nevertheless, we believe we have done a service to Bruno scholars by providing the <term>collation</term> <note>A detailed comparison of different versions of a text to identify variations</note> with the *Cambrai Acrotismus* <note>original: 'Acrotismus Camoeracensis'; a record of Bruno's public challenges to Aristotelian philosophy at the University of Paris</note>, and we were able to do so through the extreme kindness of Dr. V. Lutoslawski, who examined the only copy known thus far. Thus we also hope not to meet with disapproval for having followed the *Combinatory Lamp* <note>original: 'Lampas combinatoria'</note> with the few, insignificant, and in many places <term>corrupt</term> <note>Text that has been damaged or inaccurately transcribed over time</note> *Observations* <note>original: 'Animadversiones'</note>, instead of inserting them into the already over-large volume of unpublished works to be published in a few weeks. However small the importance of these *Observations* may be, we wish here also to express our gratitude to Professor R. Stölzle of Würzburg, who brought the precious Augsburg <term>codex</term> <note>A handwritten manuscript book</note> to our attention, and to the Librarian Dr. Dobel, who generously granted its transmission.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS

## LORD GIOVANNI MORO <note>original: "D. D. IOANNI MORO"</note>

### AMBASSADOR FOR THE MOST SERENE REPUBLIC OF VENICE <note>original: "PRO SERENISSIMA VENET. R. P."</note>

### TO THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING OF THE FRENCH AND THE POLES, <note>This refers to King Henry III, who held both titles during this period.</note>

### GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA <note>original: "IORD. BRVN. NOL."</note>

### SENDS GREETINGS. <note>original: "S. D." abbreviating "Salutem Dicit," a standard formal greeting.</note>

Any person of sound mind will judge that a **Pearl** <note>original: "Margaritam"; Bruno uses the pearl as a metaphor for his mnemonic "Art."</note> should be valued not so much for the benefit of the belly <note>That is, its raw material value or what it can be traded for to buy food.</note>, the weight of its mass, or the scale of its dimensions, as for the sight of the eyes, the substance of its own appearance, and the quality of its kind. Such a thing should be given not to just anyone, but to a man of higher nobility. <margin>10</margin> Therefore, I have judged that this art—which is incomparable to stones and gems, and all the more precious for being contained within such a small volume of books—should be dedicated not to just anyone I might meet, but to You. For the judgment and possession of such a great thing is fitting for you, O most illustrious Lord, by the shared nobility of our country and blood, <margin>2v</margin> <margin>15</margin> and by your own virtue and talent. Indeed, with such and so great a guardian, we do not fear that the irrational herd of creatures will trample this art under their feet in contempt. <note>A reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 7:6 against "casting pearls before swine."</note> Farewell.

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of Giordano Bruno's work to Giovanni Moro, the Venetian ambassador to the French court. Bruno uses the metaphor of a "pearl" to describe his mnemonic art, arguing that its intellectual and intrinsic value makes it a fit gift only for a man of Moro's high standing and intellect.</summary>

<keywords>Giordano Bruno, Giovanni Moro, Republic of Venice, dedication, King of France, Henry III, Pearl metaphor, Art of Memory, patronage</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication to Giovanni Moro into the technical treatise. ->GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA<-

# COMMENTARY ON THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE BOOKS OF LULL
<note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher and mystic who created a "Great Art" (*Ars Magna*) using logic and combinatorics to prove theological truths. Bruno was one of the most famous Renaissance "Lullists."</note>

---

### FIRST SECTION.

#### CHAPTER 1. THE PROPOSED SUBJECT. <note>original: "Q. propositum. Caput 1." The "Q" in these headings is likely an abbreviation for "Quaestio" (Question) or "Quod" (That), a common Scholastic convention.</note>

Rejecting all the vanity of bombastic speech <note>original: "sermonis ampullati," literally "puffed-up" or "swollen" language</note>, let us take up the universal and primary efficient cause, the particular and proximate agent, the material cause <margin>10</margin> which disposes the first, the subject of consideration, and finally the parts, form, and goal of this most worthy architecture and mastery.

<margin>3v</margin>
#### CHAPTER 2. THE PRIMARY EFFICIENT CAUSE.

The universal efficient cause of the Lullian art is the extrinsic active intellect. <note>In the philosophy of the time, the "active intellect" was the power that turned potential thoughts into actual knowledge. "Extrinsic" suggests it acts upon the individual mind from a higher source.</note> It relates to the illumination of the mind itself in no different a way than the daytime star <note>The Sun</note>—by whose aid all things that are seen are made visible—relates to the external <margin>15</margin> eye. By its operation, things that are first only visible in potentiality are made visible in actuality, so that from there the sensitive faculty, having been immediately stirred, is awakened and informed; the cause of that [intellect], which never...

<summary>Bruno begins his formal analysis of Lullian logic, defining the "architecture" of the system and identifying the "Active Intellect" as the primary force that illuminates the human mind, just as the sun allows the eye to see.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Lull, Active Intellect, efficient cause, illumination, architecture of logic, epistemology, Aristotelian causes</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the "efficient causes" of Ramon Lull’s system. It transitions from the general "universal" cause (the divine or extrinsic active intellect) to the "proximate" cause (the individual human mind) and the physical temperament required for such deep contemplation.</meta>

->GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA ON THE COMPENDIUM OF THE ARCHITECTURE OF LULL'S ART<-

...so that it does not fail to occur to well-inclined minds; for the rays of its brightness stand continually, as it were, at the doors of our intelligence, so that if we open our mind with a purer contemplation, they may creep deeper inside without delay, and those things that are intelligible in potentiality <margin>5</margin> may emerge into the act of intelligibility as if out of the darkness.

### Chapter 3. The Proximate Efficient Cause. <note>original: "Q. efficiens proximum."</note>

Indeed, the particular efficient cause was the Lullian active intellect <note>In medieval philosophy, the "active intellect" (intellectus agens) is the power of the mind that abstracts universal concepts from sensory data.</note>, compared and exposed to the intelligible forms and the | <margin>**239**</margin> aforementioned illuminator in the same way as each of our <margin>10</margin> eyes is to visible forms and to this sensible sun.

<margin>**4r**</margin>
### Chapter 4. The Material "In Which." <note>original: "Q. materia in qua." This refers to the physical or psychological "substrate" that allows the Art to work.</note>

The material cause, which I shall explain briefly, was a more tempered state of a certain Saturnian melancholy. <note>In the Renaissance, "Saturnian melancholy" was not merely sadness, but a specific temperament associated with the planet Saturn, believed to grant genius and the capacity for deep, solitary contemplation.</note> The <margin>15</margin> spirit residing within it offers itself to the soul as a more fit instrument for the work of contemplation, so that even someone uncultivated by any disciplines of human study (like earth more disposed toward heaven) may suddenly emerge as a wonder once the seeds have been conceived. We believe this happened to Homer, Hesiod, Zoroaster, and many <margin>20</margin> others, according to physical judgment.

### Chapter 5. The Material "About Which." <note>original: "Q. materia de qua." This refers to the subject matter or "content" of the system.</note>

The subject of consideration is the universe, which is capable of coming under the category of the true, the intelligible, and the rational. For indeed, general truths and necessary and primitive <margin>25</margin> principles are set forth to such an extent that outside of the speculative faculties, as...

<summary>Bruno defines the "efficient causes" of the Lullian Art, identifying the individual mind as the proximate agent and "Saturnian melancholy" as the ideal physical temperament for genius. He also establishes that the Art's subject matter is the entire universe and its primary, necessary truths.</summary>

For there exists no habit <note>In this context, a "habit" (habitus) refers to a stable mental disposition, skill, or branch of knowledge.</note> that can bypass the balance of these principles. It is surely | <margin>4v</margin> fitting and possible that, in the same way that meta- <margin>5</margin> physics proposes universal being—which is divided into substance and accident <note>In traditional philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself (like a person), while an "accident" is a quality that exists only in a substance (like their height or color).</note>—as its object, a certain unique and more general "being of reason" <note>original: "ens rationis"; this refers to things that exist within the mind, such as logical concepts.</note> should encompass "real being" <note>original: "ens reali"; things that exist in the physical world.</note> (through which, ultimately, a multitude of any kind can be reduced to a simple unity). <margin>10</margin>

### Chapter 6. The Dignity of the Subject Considered. <note>original: "Dignitas subiecti cons."</note>

The dignity of the matter under consideration is situated in the certainty of its attainment, in the concise ease of its treatment, in its self-sufficiency within its own kind, and in the universal nobility of the matter being | <margin>240</margin> treated. For what (even if it does not teach one to demonstrate <margin>15</margin> more expressly from definite and proper principles) does it not encompass and comprehend of the nobility of every faculty?

### Chapter 7. What the Parts of the Faculty Are. <note>original: "Q. partes facult."</note>

Two faculties are completed through the benefit of this art; hence it contains within itself two parts (which they would call "virtuative" <note>original: "virtutales." This refers to the inherent powers or capacities of a faculty to act.</note>), <margin>20</margin> of which one tends toward invention <note>In the classical rhetorical sense, "invention" is the process of finding or discovering arguments and ideas.</note>, order, arrangement, and judgment; while the other leads to that which has been invented, ordered, arranged, and judged.

### Chapter 8. What the Parts of the First Faculty Are. <margin>5r</margin> <note>original: "Q. facultatis primae partes."</note>

# ON THE CONCISE ARCHITECTURE OF LULL'S ART
<margin>2</margin>

...simple elements are enumerated and determined), he lays down the simple **intentions** <note>In medieval logic, an "intention" is a mental concept or a way the mind "intends" or points toward an object.</note> of things as if they were the most solid foundations. Second, as if creating syllables, he joins together combinations of intentions. He does this first in the **first figure**, where—with lines extending in every direction—he teaches how to relate and combine each of the **absolute predicates** <note>In Llull's system, absolute predicates are fundamental attributes such as Goodness, Greatness, Power, and Wisdom.</note> with all others, both in their abstract and concrete forms. 

<margin>5</margin> Then, in the **second figure**, he demonstrates how the **relative predicates** <note>Relative predicates describe relationships, such as "difference," "agreement," "beginning," or "equality."</note> and their corresponding scale are to be related not only to one another but also to the absolute predicates. Third, in the **third figure**, <margin>10</margin> he introduces a more distinct rule and the variations of combinations that can be formed from both types of predicates. It is here that he reveals how complete "words" are forged from the "syllables of intentions." In that place, he sets before our eyes how **propositions** are formed for <margin>15</margin> every type of question, in which any absolute or relative predicate (or a combination of them) can be affirmed or denied, proven or disproven <margin>5v</margin> regarding any subject. In this way, he seems to complete a perfect discipline of inquiry.

<margin>20</margin> ->Chapter 9. The parts of the second faculty.<-

The second part is divided into seven sections. In these, he provides instruction on how to properly produce "speeches" <note>original: "orationibus"; here Bruno uses a linguistic metaphor to describe the production of complex logical discourses or formal arguments.</note>—moving beyond the "dictionary," the "syllabary," and the "alphabet" already explained. For once those steps are completed—which pertain to the simple <margin>25</margin> conception and the first and second level of combining simple things—he moves toward the act of truly affirming and denying. In these sections, an abundant supply of arguments is contained, implicitly ready for every kind of problem.

# ON THE CONCISE ARCHITECTURE OF LULL'S ART

Likewise, the capacity for providing responses, for every kind of discourse, and for the forming of definitions, proceeds finally toward their explanation, **multiplication** <note>In this context, "multiplication" refers to the process of expanding a few basic principles into a vast number of potential arguments.</note>, and **evacuation** <note>From the Latin *evacuatio*; in Lullian logic, this refers to the systematic exhaustion of every possible combination of terms to ensure a complete analysis.</note>. He achieves this through several steps: first, by arranging the **fourth figure**, in which—as if within a golden talent <note>A "talent" was a large unit of weight or currency in antiquity; Bruno uses it here as a metaphor for a high-value container of wisdom.</note>—a manifold variety of coinage is more compactly contained; second, he provides a table in which all types of **middle terms** <term>The "middle term" is the bridge in a syllogism that connects the subject and the predicate (e.g., in "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man," "man" is the middle term).</term> are extended, explained, and numbered; third, he performs the exhaustion of the **third figure**, in which the propositions implicit in the first antecedents are unfolded; fourth, he performs the multiplication of the **fourth figure**. In this fourth stage, <margin>6r</margin> first indeed the reasons for either inferring or blocking a specific conclusion are multiplied; then, by arranging a "middle" in the central circle between the **subject** and the **predicate** (which are observed in the outer circles), the "middle terms" for constructing an argument are discovered. (I omit what is added here concerning the knowledge of **fallacies** <note>Logical errors or deceptive arguments.</note> and the excellence of this Art, since the former is irrelevant to our purpose and the latter is not strictly necessary for the practice of the Art.)

Fifth, he addresses the mixing of principles and questions. Here, by deducing these principles through those—the absolute through the relative, and both in complex or simple ways, together or one by one through a multitude of questions—the power of **invention** <term>In classical logic, "invention" (*inventio*) is the systematic method of finding or discovering valid arguments.</term> and judgment is enriched in a wondrous way. Sixth, he provides the definition of **subjects** (which I personally wish were more distinctly handled) and their diversification as they are led through different categories. This is done so that it can be determined how these subjects—and everything reduced to them as if implied within them—relate to the absolute and relative principles joined to them. This allows one to see, <margin>242</margin> from that point, how one may reason regarding **predicates** <note>A "predicate" is what is affirmed or denied about the subject of a proposition.</note> of any kind (for Llull believes all possible predicates can be reduced to these specific classes) concerning **subjects** of any kind (to which...

# ON THE COMPENDIOUS ARCHITECTURE OF THE ART OF LULL #

...for the same author feels that these <term>subjects</term> <note>original: "subiecta"; in the Lullian system, these are the fundamental categories of being, such as God, Angels, or Man</note> are reduced to all other subjects and are contained within them. By these we ought to be ruled, directed, and governed. Let it be made clear (for in this sixth part lies the chief goal of this craft, which has remained hidden from all of Lull’s interpreters, and Lull himself was least able to express it, neither in his instructions nor in his examples; but if anything can be contributed to this business, I shall provide it according to my strength, should leisure be granted); seventh, one must show the <term>application</term>, which is the primary intention (though this primary intention is barely visible because of the mixture of many useless and vain things): specifically, that all subjects are reduced to nine <term>subjects</term>, and are included and implied within them. Likewise, [it shows] how all absolute things are referred back to nine absolutes, and all relative things to the nine relative <term>predicates</term> <note>original: "praedicata"; the qualities or attributes assigned to a subject</note>. Furthermore, it shows how all knowable things—through the implicit and the explicit, the abstract and the concrete, through the provided <term>figures</term> <note>the circular diagrams used to combine concepts</note>, through <term>definitions</term>, through <term>questions</term>, through the <term>table</term>, through the <term>evacuation</term> <note>the process of systematically exhausting all possible logical combinations</note> of the third figure, through the <term>multiplication</term> of the fourth figure, through the <term>mixture of principles</term>, through the reasoning of the nine subjects, and through the <term>one hundred forms</term> <note>a specific Lullian list of metaphysical and logical concepts</note>—are constructed, examined, and formed.

### The Plan. Chapter 1.

5 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now looking not to the book, but to the art itself (which is to be elucidated and completed by us), we set forth the alphabet of the art and its memorization; likewise the <term>first figure</term> <note>Lull's "First Figure" (Figure A) usually represents the attributes of God or absolute principles like Goodness and Greatness.</note> and its image, the second figure and its easy and ready conception, the third figure and the logic of its arrangement so that it does not escape the mind of the one reasoning, the fourth figure which we form with a specific layout, and the <term>table</term> <note>The "Table" is a grid used to systematically list all possible combinations of the principles.</note> which presents itself to all with its numbers and orders in such a way that it requires no other instruction for the memory, and the <margin>7^v</margin> questions following in a natural order.

### On the Alphabet. Chapter 2.

15 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as writing and reading consist of their own elements <note>original: "elementis"; here meaning letters of the alphabet.</note>, so too do judgment and <term>discovery</term> <note>original: "inventio"; in the classical tradition, this is the art of finding or "inventing" arguments for a topic.</note>, which are attempted through this and many other arts. Therefore, the elements of this art are—not without consideration—represented by grammatical letters, which are nine in number: B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K. B itself is left as the primary letter because A is already occupied to signify the first figure. Each of these elements signifies, first of all, a <term>subject</term>...

### ON THE CONCISE ARCHITECTURE OF THE LULLIAN ART.

...absolute predicate, thirdly a relative predicate, and fourthly a question <note>Ramon Llull's "Art" (Ars) is a system of logic that uses an alphabet to represent various philosophical and theological concepts. By combining these letters, he believed one could discover all possible truths.</note>. Hence **B** signifies God, goodness, difference, and the question *whether?* **C** signifies an angel, greatness, concordance, and *what?* **D** signifies the heavens, duration or eternity <margin>5</margin> (or contrariety <note>original: "contrarietatem". This refers to things that are logically opposite.</note>), and *concerning what?* **E** signifies man, <margin>244</margin> power, principle, and *why?* **F** signifies imagination <note>original: "imaginationem". In medieval psychology, the imagination was the faculty that stored and processed sensory images.</note>, wisdom, the middle, and *how much?* **G** signifies the sensitive soul <note>original: "sensitivum". This refers to the level of the soul shared by humans and animals, responsible for perception.</note>, the will, the end, and *of what kind?* **H** signifies the vegetative soul <note>original: "vegetativum". This refers to the level of the soul found in plants, responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>, virtue, majority, and <margin>8<sup>r</sup></margin> *when?* **I** signifies the elemental world <margin>10</margin>, truth, equality, and *where?* **K** signifies the world of instruments <note>original: "instrumentativum". This category often refers to the mechanical arts, tools, or the "instrumental" soul which carries out the will's commands.</note>, glory, minority, and *how and with what?*

Assuming what was stated in *The Song of Circe* <note>original: "Cantu Circaeo". # GIORDANO BRUNO

[...they] signify equality; for "greatness" is spoken of regarding goodness and wisdom, etc., "goodness" and "wisdom" regarding greatness, etc., "the great" regarding the good and the wise, etc., and "the wise" and "the good" regarding the great, etc. <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, especially when discussing God or the First Principle, all attributes are interchangeable and equal.</note> This is indeed impossible in other [created] things, yet this figure serves them for that very reason: because one term is used as an adjective for the other, while one term taken in the abstract is joined to another taken in the concrete. 
<margin>5</margin> Hence, lines drawn from individual terms to the others signify that each of those individuals is modified by all the others: great, enduring, and powerful goodness; good, enduring, and powerful greatness; <margin>10r</margin> | good, great, and enduring power. 
<margin>10</margin> According to the condition of the subjects, such adjectival modification is completed through composition or division, or according to the angle of the triangle of the beginning, middle, or end, or of majority, minority, equality, difference, concord, or contrariety. <note>These terms—Beginning, Middle, End, Difference, Concordance, Contrariety—are the "Relative Principles" of the Lullian Art, often depicted in a triangular diagram.</note>
<margin>15</margin> 

Regarding this generality, it must be noted that these terms—as well as the concept of "being" <term>ens (existence/being)</term> which is implicit within them—do not signify in a way that is strictly finite or infinite, nor do they claim a limited or unlimited, or a created or uncreated state for themselves. For if they did, they would not be both of these things, but <margin>20</margin> only one or the other, which would then determine their formation. 
"Being" <note>original: "Ens"</note> signifying the infinite excludes everything except God; but signifying the finite, it must exclude God. Let the same reasoning apply to the "good," the "great," and the rest, all of which signify according to a concept common to material <margin>25</margin> and immaterial things, to substances and accidents, and to the finite and infinite. 
But if some (indeed even <term>Lullius (Ramon Llull, 13th-century philosopher and mystic)</term> himself) call the first three predicates "essential" and the rest "accidental," that should be understood as referring to the nature of the signifying terms, for which— <margin>247</margin> |

### On the Retention of the First Figure. Chapter 5.

Having also presupposed those things which must be held concerning the nature of subjects and adjectives, maintain a square courtyard <note>The "atrium quadratum" is a mnemonic device where concepts are placed in a mental room to be easily recalled.</note> divided into nine receptacles, the four corners of which should hold the elements, and the midpoints of the four sides the following [terms], while the last is truly the center of the square. 
<margin>10</margin>
Therefore, the eastern corner has B, the northern C, the western D, the southern E; the eastern side F, the northern side G, the western H, the southern I, and the center K. <note>In Llull's system, these letters represent divine attributes: B (Goodness), C (Greatness), D (Eternity/Duration), E (Power), F (Wisdom), G (Will), H (Virtue), I (Truth), and K (Glory).</note> There, consequently, you have a fixed order of conversions and of all denominations through individual parts, and of individual parts through all things. We despise the round figure as being an enemy to memory; we choose the angular one as being most familiar to it. <note>Bruno argued that the human mind remembers distinct angles and corners better than the uniform curve of a circle.</note>
<margin>11r</margin>

The middle row is labeled G (left), K (center), and I (right). The bottom row is labeled D (left), H (center), and E (right). The points are interconnected by a dense network of lines: the outer square perimeter; a vertical and horizontal cross through K; two main diagonals connecting the corners; an inscribed diamond shape connecting the midpoints F, I, H, and G; and additional lines connecting each corner to the two non-adjacent midpoints on the opposite sides (e.g., C is connected to I and H), forming a complex star-like pattern within the square.</image-desc>

<meta>This page continues Bruno's technical explanation of the Lullian "combinatorial" system. Having previously introduced the "Second Figure" (Figure T) and its star-like diagram, Bruno now explains why this specific figure is structured around triangles rather than the circles used in the first figure. He is detailing how different philosophical categories (like Goodness and Greatness) interact with one another.</meta>

### ON THE COMPENDIOUS ARCHITECTURE OF THE ART OF LULL.

<margin>12^r</margin>
<margin>249</margin>
It is composed not of a circle, but of three triangles; for the terms of this figure do not admit the same kind of sequence <note>meaning a logical or natural progression</note> that the terms of the first figure were said to have among themselves. For one does not speak of a "concordant difference" or a "concordant contrariety" in every possible way, though they may be spoken of in certain ways. For we say a **good beginning** differs from a **great one**, because "good" and "great" have different **definitions** <note>original: *rationes*; here referring to the conceptual structure or "reason" for a thing's existence</note>. A **good beginning** is simply the contrary of a **simply bad one**, and **great majority** <note>meaning superiority or greatness</note> differs from **glorious majority**, being the opposite of **smallness**. Behold how these predicates **penetrate** <note>a technical Lullian term for how two distinct concepts can overlap or apply to the same thing simultaneously</note> one another; this must be understood not only regarding the concepts in themselves, but also as they are grounded in subjects. For instance, when we speak of the "great, infinite, and enduring goodness of God," or the "small and finite goodness of man." The judgment regarding the other terms is the same, in its own way.

<margin>12^v</margin>
Furthermore, it consists of triangles and not a circle because the terms of the present figure do not form a single, uniform order. To anyone who considers them, three distinct orders are manifest. The first, consisting of its own triad, is called the order of **equivalence** <term>aequiparatio: a relationship between things of the same level or kind</term>; the second is by **supposition** <term>suppositio: in this context, the relationship between a subject and the properties that "stand under" or belong to it</term>; the third is by **excess and deficiency** <term>excessum et deminutionem: terms describing things that are greater or lesser than one another</term>, as the Lullian terms sound. For this reason, a figure signifying a level proportion and the same fixed relationship is judged to be least suitable. Such was the circular figure, which has all parts related uniformly and equally from every point of its circumference to the center point A, along with equal and level outflows and inflows of lines.

Finally, it consists of **acute triangles** because they "sub-enter" <note>or penetrate</note> the first figure, which is penetrable from all its angles. Hence, there is a **difference** between "good" and "good," or "good" and "great"; likewise, there is both **difference** and **contrariety** between "good" and "evil." Where a **sensible good** <note>something perceived as good by the senses, like food</note> and an **intelligible evil** <note>something understood as evil by the mind, like a lie</note> differ only in kind, a **sensible good** and a **sensible evil** are directly contrary to one another.

<summary>Bruno explains that the "Second Figure" of the Lullian system uses triangles to map complex relationships like difference and opposition, which are too nuanced for a simple circular diagram. He distinguishes between how things differ in kind (equivalence) versus how they differ in degree (excess and deficiency).</summary>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

<margin>20</margin>
The sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note> and the intelligible <note>knowable by the mind</note>, the differing and the concordant, and the remaining predicates, penetrate the first figure and embrace each other. Along with the angles of other triangles, these are no less grounded in their subjects than they are abstract <note>original: "exempta," referring to concepts considered apart from their physical manifestations</note>. Indeed, <margin>5</margin> categorized by difference, concordance, contrariety, beginning, middle, end, majority, minority, and equality, these subjects are God, Spirit <note>original: "Daemon," here referring to the Neoplatonic concept of an intermediary being between humans and gods, rather than an evil entity</note>, Heaven, Man, and the rest, and those things which are reduced to these subjects. They also <margin>250</margin> penetrate and embrace the subjects no less denominatively <note>referring to an attribute or quality, e.g., "divine"</note> <margin>10</margin> than when they are taken absolutely <note>referring to the essence itself, e.g., "God"</note>; absolutely, I say: God, Angel, <margin>13r</margin> Heaven, Man; denominatively: divine, angelic, celestial, human.

# ON THE COMPREHENSIVE ARCHITECTURE OF THE LULLIAN ART.

### On the Third Figure. Chapter 8.

The third figure is not represented by any single letter or element; indeed, it seems to be nothing other than the combination **251** <note>This refers to the page number in an early edition of Bruno's works</note> of the first figure with the second. Its elements signify whatever the elements of the first and the elements of the second signify.
<margin>15</margin> We note that this figure possesses many modes of "inflexion" <note>Permutations or logical combinations used to generate new ideas</note> that are extremely useful for creating an abundance of subject matter. The first of these is when an absolute term <note>Essential qualities like Goodness or Greatness</note> is taken as the subject and another absolute term as the predicate, such as when we say, "great goodness." Second, when both terms are relative <note>original: "respectivis," referring to terms like Difference or Concordance that describe relationships</note>, as when we say <margin>20</margin> "beginning difference," "mediating concordance," or "ending contrariety." Third, when an absolute term is used as the subject and a relative term as the predicate, as in saying "differing goodness." Fourth, when a relative term is the subject and an absolute term is the predicate, as in saying "good difference." These four <margin>25</margin> modes are multiplied: first, by taking the subject or predicate either as an adjective or a noun <note>original: "adiective... substantive"</note>, saying "great goodness," "good greatness," "beginning difference," "differing <margin>14v</margin> principle," "differing goodness," "good difference"; and second, when both...

### On the fourth figure. Chapter 10.

The fourth figure, consisting of three concentric circles, encompasses the three preceding figures. It is designed for the construction of the **general table** <note>original: "tabulae generalis"; this refers to the master grid used in Lullian logic to organize all possible knowledge</note>. By its help, a person skilled in this art will be able to multiply solutions and arguments for the same problem in infinite ways.

<image-desc>A circular Lullian diagram (volvelle) composed of three concentric rings. Each ring is partitioned into nine segments, each containing a letter of the Lullian alphabet: B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, and K, arranged in clockwise order. The letters are aligned radially across the three rings to form nine spokes. A central dot marks the axis of rotation.</image-desc>

<margin>17r</margin>
The present figure has seven revolutions <note>referring to the shifting of the rings to create new combinations</note>, by which seven **chambers** <term>domus: literally "houses," these are the cells or groupings within the combinatorial table</term> are successively established. The first of these is established when, under the letter B of the upper, immobile circle, is placed... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the end of the folio.</note>

### The seventh house of one chamber.

The seventh house is formed by moving, under H of the fixed circle, I of the middle circle and K of the lowest. <note>In Bruno’s system, the "fixed circle" is the outermost wheel of a memory device, and the "middle" and "lowest" are concentric wheels nested inside it.</note>

Therefore, from the revolution of the circles of the fourth figure, twenty-eight houses result. <note>The "fourth figure" is a Lullian device used to find relationships between concepts by rotating wheels with alphabetical notations.</note> Of these houses, the first has seven rows and 24 chambers; <note>original: "24. cameras"; likely a scribal error for 28, as noted in the textual variants below.</note> the second has six rows and 21 chambers; <margin>10</margin> the third has five rows and 15 chambers; the fourth has four rows and 10 chambers; the fifth has three rows and 6 chambers; the sixth has two rows and 3 chambers; and the seventh has one chamber. <note>A "chamber" (*camera*) is a specific combination of three letters representing a mnemonic locus.</note>

### On the Great Table. Chapter 11.

The Great Table consists of eighty-four columns, <margin>15</margin> corresponding to the total number of chambers found in the 28 rows within the seven houses, which are established by the seven revolutions in the fourth figure. <note>84 is the sum of the chambers: 28+21+15+10+6+3+1=84.</note>

Furthermore, each column consists of 21 cylinders, and each of these consists of four members. Thus, the number four <margin>20</margin> multiplied by 21 yields 84 members.

The 21 cylinders are: BCD. CBD. DBC. BBC. BBD. CCB. CCD. DDB. DDC. BCC. BDD. CBB. CDD. DBB. DCC. BCB. BDB. CBC. CDC. DBD. DCD. <note>A "cylinder" is a further subdivision of the mnemonic system, likely representing a specific phonetic or conceptual grouping.</note>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

<page-num>30</page-num>

Each of the cylinders, through the fourfold positioning of the letter **T** itself, takes on four members; for **T** is either placed before the first element **TBCD**, or after the first and before the second **BTCD**, <margin>19v</margin> or after the second and before the third **BCTD**, or after the third **BCDT**. <note>In the Lullian system Bruno is adapting, 'T' is a functional letter used to relate other concepts. Its position changes the logical meaning of the combination.</note> Elements placed before the **T** signify absolute predicates, <note>Absolute predicates are the "Dignities of God" or fundamental qualities like Goodness, Greatness, and Duration.</note> while elements placed after the **T** signify relative predicates. <note>Relative predicates describe the relationships between things, such as Difference, Concordance, or Contrariety.</note>

the sign is doubled in those cases which are denoted in the column by the addition of stars. The first set of twelve is drawn from the first three cylinders; the second from the six following; the third from the final twelve.
<margin>5</margin> This column of 84 members <note>The original Latin text says 84, but a correction suggests it should be 88, as Bruno calculates elsewhere.</note>—of which we have said 36 are useful—is more fertile than the Lullian column <note>Referring to the system of Raymond Lull (Raymundus Lullus), a Catalan philosopher who invented a logical machine consisting of paper wheels.</note>, which consists of only 20 **260** members in a single cylinder. It happened, however, that we enriched it using the same logic by which Raymond might have omitted the other members; he saw the repetition of the same thing as useless.
<margin>10</margin> For instance, to say **BCD**, which stands for "enduring great goodness," and to say **CBD**, which stands for "enduring good greatness," appeared to him to be the same thing. We, however, do not reject Raymond’s order or his sufficiency, and we admit that in his group of twenty **22^r**
<margin>15</margin> everything is ultimately contained—but blindly, and perhaps even hidden from or less considered by Lull himself. Therefore, after we have extended the combinations that can be made from these four ordered elements, and after it has been revealed which among them are fruitful, let the column be traversed by taking the first element substantively <term>substantively: using the concept as a noun or the primary subject</term> and the remaining
<margin>20</margin> two adjectivally <term>adjectivally: using the concepts as modifiers or qualities</term>, saying: "Great enduring goodness," which is signified by **BCD**. Would not another arrangement of these same elements be extremely useful—and even necessary for completing the discourse—by saying: "Good enduring greatness," for which the
<margin>25</margin> sign is **CBD**? This is certainly not a repetition of the same thing. Similarly, there will never be a repetition if the three terms are arranged by a certain law through adjectives and substantives, or through direct and oblique cases <note>original: "rectum et obliquum," referring to grammatical cases like the nominative vs. possessive/objective, which change the logical relationship between the words.</note>, so that one member relates to another by that same law, or if all members are taken in a uniform manner.

# ON THE COMPACT ARCHITECTURE OF THE ART OF LULLY

...[in this way], there will never be a repetition of the same thing, and we will not fall into the omission of a necessary element, just as when **BCD** is established, **CBD** is disregarded <note>original: "necessarii omissionem... BCD contemnitur CBD". Bruno is arguing that his system captures nuances that earlier logicians like Lull might have ignored as redundant.</note>.

### The Number of Laws.

<margin>22v</margin>
The laws, truly, by which the column is uniformly traversed, are eight: 1. one is by taking the first term adjectivally <term>adjectivally: using the term as a quality or modifier (e.g., "good")</term>, and the remaining two substantively <term>substantively: using the term as the primary subject or noun (e.g., "goodness")</term>; 2. another is by taking the first term substantively, and the other two adjectivally; 3. another by taking the first and second terms adjectivally, and the third substantively; 4. another by taking the first and second terms substantively, and the third adjectivally; 
<margin>261</margin>
5. another by taking the first and third adjectivally, and the second substantively; (6.) another by taking the first and third substantively, and the second adjectivally; 7. another by taking all terms adjectivally; 8. and another by taking all terms substantively.

### Multiplication of the Laws.

The aforementioned eight laws, through the varied distribution of the oblique and the direct, the abstract and the concrete <note>These are technical terms from Latin grammar used here to describe how the logical concepts relate to one another in a sentence structure.</note>, establish thirty-eight highly useful considerations of propositions <note>The source manuscript note suggests there may actually be 39 combinations in practice, despite Bruno’s count of 38.</note> by which a given problem can be examined.

For when the first term stands adjectivally, and the second and third substantively, it is said:

The duration of greatness of good. <note>original: "Boni magnitudinis duratio."</note>

->The multiple ways of receiving terms.<-

Nor should it escape your notice that the first term, signified in this place—that is, in this column—by B, is sometimes taken <margin>15</margin> by itself, such as when the question concerns **goodness**; sometimes it is taken with another term used simply, such as when the question concerns the **goodness of the world**, the **good of nature**, or the **highest good**; and sometimes it is taken with another term used complexly, as when the question concerns the **goodness of the eternity of the world**. ### On the Questions. Chapter 13.

Ten questions (to which Lullus <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the philosopher who invented this combinatorial system</note> wishes all others to be reduced) have been listed, and we have assigned these to be signified by nine elements <note>referring to the letter-symbols B through K used in the Lullian diagrams</note>. <margin>10 **25<sup>v</sup>**</margin> Lullus says he calls these "rules" for this reason: just as all words are encompassed by the rules of the five Latin declensions, so too, in their own way, are all possible questions included in these ten. These are the elements that survey, illuminate, and color everything, if the full weight of a question is to be properly considered. <margin>15</margin>Of these, four are naturally **substantial** <term>substantial: relating to the essence or "what" a thing is</term>: **B** whether it is, **C** what it is, **D** from what it is, **E** why it is; and seven are **accidental** <term>accidental: relating to qualities, timing, or circumstances rather than essence</term>: **F** how much, **G** what kind, **H** when, **I** where, **K** how and with what.

<margin>5</margin> The seventh subject, which is the Vegetative <term>Vegetativum: the biological power of growth, nutrition, and reproduction common to plants, animals, and humans</term>, embraces the elemental as though it were its trunk and foundation; for the disposition of the Vegetative follows the disposition of the element, just as the disposition of the Sensitive follows that of the Vegetative, and the Imaginative follows that, and finally the actually Intellectual <note>Bruno is describing a "Great Chain of Being" where each higher level of soul depends on the physical and biological layers beneath it</note>. Therefore, the nature of the higher subject <margin>**30<sup>v</sup>**</margin> <margin>10</margin> includes the nature of the lower subject, either as a composite, or as something informed <note>given "form" or life by a higher principle</note>, or as a participant, or as something participated in, or as an agent, or as a certain kind of subject <margin>**270**</margin>. The essence of this subject rests upon vital powers, namely the appetitive <note>the drive to seek nourishment</note>, the attractive <note>the ability to draw in nutrients</note>, the retentive <note>the ability to hold and preserve matter</note>, the digestive, the expul<margin>15</margin>sive, and the similar productive <note>reproductive</note> power. All these things, both together and individually, should be referred to the circumference of questions and predicates, and to those things which follow from them, according to the abundance of things.

### On the eighth subject. I.

The eighth subject, which is the Elementative <term>Elementativum: the realm of the four physical elements—earth, air, fire, and water—and their underlying qualities</term>, com<margin>20</margin>prises the natural Instrumentative, which illuminates, touches, and penetrates all things. And let this subject be considered according to its essence and the faculties and acts that follow from it. This is imagined by some to be fourfold <note>referring to the four classical elements</note>, by others twofold, by others infinitely manifold, but by those with better understanding, it is seen as simple. <margin>25</margin> Such it is according to Lull <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), the Catalan philosopher whose system of revolving wheels and combinatorial logic Bruno adapted</note>, who calls it Chaos <term>Chaos: not "disorder" in the modern sense, but the primal, undifferentiated "prime matter" from which the elements emerge</term>, the composition of which...

...is composed of prime matter <term>prima materia: the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe from which all things are made</term> and the form most immediate to it. By considering their essence, being, differences, species, virtues, acts, and circumstances from the center of the circle of predications <note>original: "praedicationum" — referring to the circular diagrams in Lull's Art used to make logical assertions</note>, we shall have no small material for contemplation.

<margin>10</margin> ### On the ninth subject. K.

The ninth subject, which is the Instrumental <term>Instrumentativum: the tools of logic and law used to organize and understand other subjects</term>, is twofold: namely, natural and moral. The first encompasses the nine categories of accidents <note>original: "accidentium genera" — in Aristotelian logic, these are the nine ways a thing can be described beyond its essential substance, such as its size, color, or location</note>, so that all remaining beings besides the eight previously mentioned (which belong to the category of substance) may be <margin>15</margin> included. Therefore, the instrumental subject consists of quantity, quality, relation, and the rest, with their species, differ- | ences, properties, and commonalities, which are treated <margin>**271**</margin> partly by the logician and partly by the metaphysician. # GIORDANO BRUNO

All absolute predicates, according to Llull, are reduced to these <term>praedicata: the attributes or qualities assigned to a subject in logic</term> either affirmatively or negatively, according to one mode or another. If anyone wishes to arrange them in order, they should do so by reducing them to the distinct halls <note>original: "atria"—Bruno envisions the logical categories as physical spaces or chambers in a memory palace</note> of these principles. In all predications, however, the steps of the ladder <margin>5</margin> of the intellect should be recalled to memory: namely, the <margin>32v</margin> most specific, the subaltern <note>intermediate categories</note>, and the most general. These represent the "height" of the subject, serving as the highest, middle, and lowest points. Likewise, one must consider their differences, properties, and the specific, appropriate reasons that follow their essence—these constitute the "breadth" of the ladder. Sometimes these should be taken simply, and at other times complexly in relation to each other and to others. For instance, one might say "difference, principle, contrary"; or one might say <margin>15</margin> "contrasting difference, principal difference, concordant principle," and so on. Indeed, they can even be combined with the subjects themselves: divine goodness, angelic goodness, celestial goodness, human goodness, and so forth.

### On the expansion and numbering of the second figure. Chapter III.

The second figure reveals its own scope in its description and diagram. For each of the principles proposes itself to be <margin>20</margin> examined by three differences. If, for example, the "difference" of the soul <note>original: "animae differentia"</note> should be considered, one must look at what exists between the soul and the sensible, and between the soul and the intelligible <term>intelligible: things known by the mind/intellect rather than the five senses</term>, as is signified in the "angle of difference." The same judgment applies to the other <margin>33r</margin> angles. This difference is subsequently formed <margin>25</margin> through the other angles of this figure—namely, majority, minority, principle, middle, and end—together with the species and modes indicated in the ladders of the angles.

# ON THE CONCISE ARCHITECTURE OF LLULL'S ART.

Difference is also formed through the absolute predicates <note>original: "absoluta praedicata"—the fundamental qualities like Goodness or Greatness that describe the nature of a thing</note> of the first figure, by deriving the "difference" of the soul from other things according to its goodness, its greatness, its duration, and the rest. <margin>273</margin> Similarly, this applies to concordance and majority; likewise regarding the species <note>sub-categories</note> and modes of these, along with those genera, species, and their specific modes. If all these cannot be established affirmatively, let them be tested negatively, according to every possible mode of negation.

### On expansion through the third figure. Chapter IV.

The third figure encompasses the scope of the first and second figures. The elements <note>The letters B through K used as variables in Llull's system</note> of this figure signify what is both implicit and explicit in the "alphabet," in the subjects, and in the two preceding figures and questions. For in the letter **B** of this figure is signified: God (as the first subject), Goodness (as the first absolute predicate), Difference (as the first relative predicate), Justice <margin>33v</margin> (as the first of the virtues), Avarice (as the first of the vices), and "Whether" (as the first of the questions). A similar judgment applies to the letters **C, D, E, F, G, H, I,** and **K**. Therefore, each of the elements of this figure possesses seven meanings, and each of the combined squares <note>In Llull's diagrams, letters are paired into cells or "squares" to find logical connections</note> encompasses fourteen meanings.

In the first square, therefore, which is **BC**, many inquiries and problems are included to be contemplated, aimed at, and applied to any given purpose. This is done first through two terms, of which one is a "question" and the other is an "absolute predicate"—for example: "Whether goodness exists?" or "What is goodness?" Alternatively, one might be a relative predicate: "Whether difference exists?" or "What is difference?" Finally, by touching upon the scales of the angles <note>original: "angulorum scalas"—referring to the geometric connections in the Lullian diagram</note>: "Whether there is a difference between the sensible and the intelligible <note>Sensible refers to things perceived by the senses; intelligible refers to things understood by the mind</note>, and what it is, and..."

Bruno demonstrates how the letter 'B' serves as a shorthand for multiple philosophical categories across different moral and logical scales.</summary>

### On the amplification, multiplication, and order of questions. Chapter VI.

<margin>5</margin> The method for expanding questions is not by restricting them to a specific field of study, but—since they must relate to everything in their own way—by understanding them according to the broadest possible meaning, so that they can be applied to all things collectively and individually as their nature requires. From this:

<margin>10</margin>
#### B. On the amplification and multiplication of the question "Whether." <note>In Llull's system, the question "Whether" (Latin: *Utrum*) is the first step of inquiry, asking if a thing exists or is possible.</note>

The question "Whether" is expanded and multiplied through the assertive, the affirmative, the doubtful, and the negative; the probable, the apparent, and the demonstrative; the believed, the reasoned, and the understood. Likewise, it refers to all questions concerning being and essence, and to those reducible to them.

"Whether" is expanded just as other questions proposed for expansion are, by taking it in a wider sense than is customary among theologians. For the philosopher asks whether God exists and similar things, about which a theologian <margin>276</margin> <margin>20</margin> should have no doubt at all, as Ramon [Llull] notes in his *Rhetoric*. <margin>36r</margin> This very question "Whether" was the reason Moses did not enter the Promised Land; for God punished him for that reason, because when he struck the rock he said: "Is God here or not?" <note>original: "estne Deus an non?" Bruno refers to the biblical episode in Numbers 20:12 where Moses' hesitation or lack of faith at Meribah is interpreted as a "Whether" question.</note>

<margin>25</margin>
#### C. On the amplification and multiplication of the question "What." <note>The question "What" (Latin: *Quid*) seeks the definition or essence of the subject established by the previous question.</note>

The question "What" is expanded so that it is common to both the demonstrative <note>Logical proof based on certain premises.</note> and the persuasive <note>Rhetorical proof based on probability.</note>. It is answered not only through the properties of the thing—

[the question "What" provides answers] not only through direct definitions, but also through circumlocutions and metaphorical or figurative definitions and descriptions throughout the universe. Hence, to one asking "what is old age?" the answer is "a harbor of evils"; to "what is it to have a most beautiful wife?" the answer is "to have golden shackles"; and to "what is the sun?" "the eye of the world." The question "What" is expanded by testing every mode of defining—from the name, from the thing itself, from the way it is conceived, and from its mode of being; likewise through what it is in itself and what it is in another, and what it possesses in itself versus what it possesses in another.

->(D.) On the expansion and multiplication of the question "Of What."<-

<margin>36v</margin> The question "Of What" <note>Latin: *De quo*. This question usually investigates the origin, material, or ownership of a subject.</note> is extended to signify essential, original, intrinsic, extrinsic, efficient, material, primitive, and possessed or positive principles. It embraces the point of origin <note>Latin: *a quo*</note> and other terms which that point presupposes, and it encompasses every composition, whether it be natural, rational, or imaginary. Finally, principles of possession according to common usage—such as the questions "whose is it?", "to whom does it belong?", and "to whom is it of interest?"—should be referred to the question "Of What."

Llull often focused on more spiritual or active causes.</note>, it nevertheless, when taken and considered in a certain way, possesses a kind of efficiency regarding change and those things that follow from change. Among these causes, some are determined, while others are indeterminate in their acting, <margin>277</margin>

# THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO

<margin>5, 10, 15, 20, 37r</margin> ...some are natural, some are voluntary, some exist through themselves <note>Latin: *per se*</note>, and others by accident <note>Latin: *per accidens*</note>. Hence, the reason "why something is" is taken first from the account of the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> of God; of fate, which signifies His immutable decree; of fortune, which signifies an uncertain and rare cause regarding things that act by choice; and of chance, to which all natural composite things can be subject.

Second, it is taken from the account of nature as an efficient cause, either through equivocal principles <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "equivocal" cause is one where the cause is of a different kind than the effect, such as the sun (cause) producing heat in a stone (effect).</note>—namely through superior natural things, such as when nature generates, produces, and moves inferior things through the heavens and the stars—or through univocal principles <note>A "univocal" cause is one where the cause and effect are of the same kind, such as a human begetting a human.</note>—namely through inferior natural things, when a like thing is generated and produced by its like and by the same in genus or species. Or it may be taken intrinsically through the form of the thing, which admits the account of an internal efficient cause; indeed, if considered in another way—namely as a part of the thing that limits matter to a certain species—it is a genus of cause distinct from the efficient cause. 

Third, it is taken by the account of the efficient cause of the will, which is distinguished into the animate will—which is twofold, being either rational or irrational—and the natural will. The natural will is realized in "prime matter" <note>The most basic, formless substance of the universe.</note> and the composite subject in respect to its most immediate and lowest form, as well as its remote and superior form. 

Fourth, it is taken from the account of the end <note>The *finis* or "final cause"—the purpose for which a thing exists.</note>, which is distinguished into the intermediate and the ultimate, the tool and the work, and that which is directly intended versus that which is indirectly intended; these six modes are distinct to anyone who considers them more deeply.

->F. On the expansion and multiplication of the question "How much."<-

<margin>25, 37v</margin>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...the category distinguished from the other nine, which is properly called "When"; likewise through a higher mode, beyond the category itself and more than transcendental, by which believers ask "when did God create time together with the heavens?" and answer themselves "in the beginning." This "beginning" is neither time, nor a part of time, nor a limit—even according to those believers—nor is it understood to exist within the category of "when," <margin>38v</margin> nor is it accepted as something that wanders through the other categories. It is not past, nor future, nor a present that joins them, nor can it be counted among those species such as yesterday, last month, <margin>279</margin> a year, once, now, sometime, and similar terms, as is manifest to one who considers it rightly. This question H <note>In the Lullian system of logic used by Bruno, "H" represents the question *Quando* (When).</note> is further expanded through the species of questions C, D, and K <note>C (What/Quid), D (From what/De quo), and K (With what/Cum quo).</note>; for something is *there* where its quidditative <note>Relating to the "quiddity" or the essential "whatness" of a thing.</note> and material constituents are, as well as its general forming and accompanying elements.

### I. On the expansion and multiplication of the question "Where" <note>Latin: *Ubi*.</note>.

The question "Where" is dilated both through the differences of place—which is a species of continuous quantity—and through the differences, species, modes, properties, and commonalities of the category distinct from the other nine, which is properly called "When" <note>Original: *Quando*. This appears to be a slip in the original text or transcription; contextually, Bruno is defining the category of *Ubi* (Where).</note>. For although God is "somewhere" in neither of the first two ways, nothing prevents one from asking where He is, <margin>39r</margin> or where He was before the world was made. They say He is, and was, in Himself; which is the same as saying: He is and was Himself; likewise as if saying: He is He; or even: I do not know, He Himself knows. This mode of responding...

...re". <margin>10</margin> ->K. On the expansion and multiplication of the question "How" <note>Latin: *Quomodo*.</note>.<-

The question "How" is expanded through all the modes by which a thing is said to relate in some way—either in itself or in another, by being or by operating—according to its own properties or those attributed to it, through modifying and being modified, in respect to an <margin>15</margin> active or passive faculty. This question indeed, just as <column-break/> others, surveys all <margin>280 39v</margin> things in its own way. For nothing prevents our theologians from asking how God differs from other beings—or indeed from [the category of] beings altogether—and how He understands Himself and, by understanding, produces. These questions are followed by <margin>20</margin> others, which neither they themselves nor others understand, just as is confessed among them. It is certain, however, that when "How" itself is applied to the First Subject [God], it cannot be reduced to any category of predication <note>The Aristotelian categories used to describe reality.</note>, except according to a very remote (or rather dissimilar, if they permit me to <margin>25</margin> say so) likeness.

From this, one may see how the breadth of this faculty encompasses the scope of logic <term>logices</term> and metaphysics <term>metaphysices</term>.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

The questions "how," "what kind," and "what" examine the differences between things of logic and things of metaphysics. They distinguish those things that rise above what is called <term>real being and being of reason</term> <note>Scholastic terms: "real being" refers to things that exist in the physical world; "being of reason" refers to things that exist only in the mind, like "nothingness" or "universals."</note> in every possible way. The same applies to absolute and relative predicates, as well as the logic behind the combinations formed by them. Although this was pointed out earlier, because this line of thought is so significant, it must be revisited again and | again, **40r** whenever the opportunity arises.

The question "With what" <note>This refers to the Lullian question K, used to explore the associations or instruments of a subject.</note> extends to everything that acts as a medium, a sign, an instrument, or as something concurrent and accompanying—whether it performs the same action or allows it to happen. It also extends through everything it transmits into, everything it receives from, and everything it transmits and receives simultaneously. Thus, nothing escapes the clarity and "coloring" <note>Bruno uses "coloration" to mean the specific character or quality a question gives to an investigation.</note> of this question.

->How all the questions are included within the Categories—understood both logically and metaphysically beyond their standard use—and vice versa. Chapter VII.<-

If anyone, moved by Aristotle's authority, thinks it sacrilege to say this, let them read and consider what Aristotle himself—led by his conscience—said at the end of the chapter *On Relation* <note>original: "De relatione"; Bruno refers to Aristotle's *Categories*, Chapter 7, where Aristotle admits the difficulty of defining certain relations.</note>; and let them realize that what was said regarding the purpose of that specific category should also be considered said regarding the purpose of all the other categories as well. I refrain from presenting a second and better reason for this, lest I incur the magisterial indignation of nitpickers and <term>sophists</term> <note>Philosophers or teachers who use clever but deceptive or fallacious arguments.</note>.

<margin>41r</margin>
The multiplication and extension that occurs through forms, we shall reorganize elsewhere—both regarding what pertains to number, what pertains to species, and what pertains to their underlying principles. For out of a desire to complete a <term>hundred</term> <note>Lull often organized his systems into "centuries" or sets of 100 to provide a sense of mathematical completeness, even if the content became repetitive.</note>, Lull repeated many things, doubled many others, and added many that are irrelevant to the matter; how this came to be, I leave for others to judge. But let these remarks suffice regarding the sufficiency of Lull’s "architecture." What Lull perhaps imagined regarding the forms, we shall omit.

These things are sufficient for understanding, judging, and pursuing the art of Lull for those who are skilled in common philosophy. For here is expressed in its entirety whatever Lull contains in his many *Arts*, in which the same thing is always...

# RAYMOND LULL

## ON THE DEFINITION OF DISPUTATION AND ITS CONDITIONS.

---

### What a disputation is. Chapter I.

5 &emsp; A disputation <note>A formal academic debate or logical argument used to uncover truth.</note> is a spiritual opposition <note>original: "contrarietas spiritualis"; here "spiritual" refers to a mental or intellectual process rather than a religious one—an encounter between minds.</note> which, through the word, manifests a conception that one intellect holds against another.

### On the conditions of disputation. Chapter II.

#### First condition.

10 &emsp; A disputant must first have the intention of knowing and loving the truth, and of knowing and hating falsehood; because of this, a true disputant must grant known truths and deny falsehoods.

#### Second condition.

<margin>42v</margin>
15 &emsp; Secondly, it should be assumed at the start that either side of the question is possible—namely, both the affirmative and the negative—so that the intellect may be free and not bound <note>In a proper logical inquiry, the thinker must not be biased or "locked" into an answer before the evidence is weighed.</note> in its investigation.

---

5. p. 64, 8 = Lull (1598 edition) p. 168 &emsp; 16 namely [scilicet]] abbreviated as *s.* in manuscript P; *or* [sive] in manuscript G.

### THE SEAL OF SEALS <note>original: "Sigillus Sigillorum"</note>

->THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO<-

Socrates called [it] a certain <note>The previous page likely referred to "forgetfulness" or "blankness" in the mind.</note> [state]; if he had, by the same logic, called the "thrown seed" of a memorable thing that was not conceived by the memory a kind of "non-sensation," he would have truly explained a much deeper matter.

20. Therefore, unless the <term>imagination</term><note>original: "phantasia"; in Bruno's time, this was the mental faculty that processed sensory images before they reached the intellect.</note> knocks quite vividly with sensible <term>forms</term><note>original: "speciebus"; the mental "images" or "likenesses" of objects.</note>, thought will not open the door; and if thought, acting as the gatekeeper, does not open up, the <margin>d 2r</margin> Mother of the Muses <note>The "Mother of the Muses" is Mnemosyne, the personification of Memory in Greek mythology.</note> will indignantly refuse to receive them.

21. Let those things be stirred up, therefore, which—accompanied by the flow of reason, thought, and a strong imagination—move the **emotions**. <note>original: "affectus"; Bruno argues that we remember best what we feel strongly about.</note> Through these, we are affected by the form of the thing to be remembered: whether we are being zealous, contemptuous, loving, hating, mourning, rejoicing, wondering, or referring things to the "scales of the senses"—along with the specific forms of zeal, contempt, love, hatred, mourning, joy, wonder, and scrutiny. Furthermore, the stronger and more vehement these emotions are, the more powerfully they leave an impression as a consequence.

22. If your own nature, or the nature of the thing you are <unclear>ar...</unclear> <note>The manuscript breaks off here; likely "apprehending" or "grasping" (Latin: *apprehendis*).</note>

<summary>This title page and introductory text establish Giordano Bruno's "Art of Memory," emphasizing that for information to be remembered, it must first be transformed into vivid mental images and energized by strong human emotions.</summary>

This not ignoble offspring of the Muses, brought forth in your most celebrated hall, is consecrated to you, most illustrious lord. I do this so that those who are indebted to me may know they are indebted to the Muses; and those who are indebted to the Muses may recognize that they are bound to you, their perpetual patron and protector. For the Muses themselves, for whom every soil is a homeland, found a French—and indeed a royal—hospitality <margin>a 2v</margin> through an Italian foster-son <note>Bruno is referring to himself as the "Italian foster-son" of the Muses.</note> here in secluded Britain, lest they should be held as foreigners anywhere or find themselves to be strangers. <margin>5</margin>Philotheus <note>original: "Philotheus" — a name Bruno frequently used for himself, meaning "Lover of God."</note> Giordano Bruno of Nola, a doctor of a more refined theology, a professor of a purer and harmless wisdom, a philosopher known, approved, and honorably received in the chief universities of Europe, a stranger nowhere except among barbarians and the ignoble, a waker of <margin>10</margin>sleeping souls, a tamer of presumptuous and recalcitrant ignorance, who in all his actions professes a universal love for humanity <term>philanthropy: used here to mean a cosmopolitan affection for all people regardless of nationality</term>, who values an Italian no more than a Briton, a male more than a female, a bishop wearing a mitre more than a king wearing a crown, a man in a robe more than one in armor, a cowled monk <margin>15</margin>more than a man without a cowl; but rather, he loves the person | whose conduct is more peaceful, **a 3^v** civil, faithful, and useful.
