<meta>This page continues the dedication to the University of Oxford. Bruno is moving from his self-introduction to a sharp critique of his detractors—specifically those who use religious piety as a shield for their lack of intellectual rigor. He uses various biblical citations sarcastically to show how his opponents justify their ignorance.</meta>

**PREFACE TO THE THIRTY SEALS.**
a 4ʳ

...the studious love, and whom the more noble minds applaud, to the most excellent and most illustrious Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford, along with the foremost members of that same university, sends his best greetings.

<margin>5</margin> There exist, most excellent lords, those who—although they clearly understand (as we do not deny) that the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God <note>original: "sapientiam huius mundi stultitiam esse apud Deum" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:19, often used by anti-intellectuals to dismiss philosophy</note>—hate all speculative disciplines and study nothing. Since it is widely accepted among them that the works of our own justice are like <margin>10</margin> filthy rags <note>original: "menstruata" — literally "menstruated [cloths]," a common biblical metaphor from Isaiah 64:6 for human righteousness compared to divine purity</note>, and that through them no one is justified before God, they do nothing good. Meanwhile, however, lest they be considered wicked and ignorant, they suddenly become learned without study, according to that saying: "You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to the little ones." <note>Matthew 11:25</note> Likewise, they are made <margin>14</margin> righteous without any good actions of their own, according to: "You, O Lord, are my righteousness." The most criminal among them are also transformed into holy, clean, and pure beings, according to: "They have been made white in the blood of the Lamb." <note>Revelation 7:14</note> Finally, though they are fools, most ignoble and infamous, they claim for themselves every kind of nobility, according to: "You are a chosen generation of God and a royal priesthood." <note>1 Peter 2:9</note> <margin>20</margin> Truly, I fear such "little ones," the "righteous," the "pure," the "bright," the "chosen," the "kings," the "priests," and "demigods"—who are capable of piercing our simplicity right to the center of the soul—more than death itself. Therefore, lest that sort of people should clash with me on any fair and legal ground, <margin>25</margin> I protest before your Excellency: while we bring forth the fruits of our inventions, offering precepts most useful for all functions of the mind—where, for the sake of obtaining the theory and practice of these things, [we look] to the methods of Pythagoras, Parmenides, Anaxagoras...

---

-> 2 academy [spelled *achademiae*]   5 most excellent   11 Meanwhile   19 according to   26 most useful <-
-> most useful] *compare to similar usage on page 34, line 21, etc.* <-

<summary>In this dedication to Oxford's leadership, Bruno sarcastically attacks religious "anti-intellectuals" who use scripture to justify their ignorance and lack of good works. He contrasts their "instant" holiness with his own rigorous philosophical pursuit of wisdom based on ancient traditions like those of Pythagoras.</summary>

<keywords>Oxford University, Vice-Chancellor, religious hypocrisy, anti-intellectualism, philosophy vs theology, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Anaxagoras, justification by faith</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the preface to Giordano Bruno's "Thirty Seals" (Triginta Sigilli), a work focused on the art of memory and philosophical inquiry. Here, Bruno addresses his critics and defines his philosophical stance against the academic establishment.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO’S PREFACE TO THE THIRTY SEALS

<sig>a 4v</sig>

...[of Pytha]goras <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "-gorae," completing the name of Pythagoras, the ancient Greek philosopher who heavily influenced Bruno's ideas on the soul and the universe.</note> and of better philosophers, whether we seem to drift toward approving their opinions or introducing our own new positions—if these appear to oppose the common and approved faith, let it be understood that these things are put forward by us not as absolutely true, but as more in harmony with the senses and our reason, or at least less discordant than the opposing side of the contradiction. 

<margin>5</margin>And let them recall this: that we do not presume so much on our own knowledge as we are moved by a love for exposing the weakness of the **common philosophy** <note>original: "vulgatae philosophiae." Bruno refers to the Aristotelian scholasticism dominant in 16th-century universities, which he viewed as rigid and outdated.</note>, which forces upon us things believed absolutely as if they were demonstratively proven. 

<margin>10</margin>Through our discussions (if the Gods grant it), it may appear how much those ideas—which are rejected as alien to the senses by the chattering crowd of common philosophers—actually correspond to regulated sense and harmonize with the truth of the substance of things. 

<margin>15</margin>Meanwhile, I would not wish that, just as it is said that in the time of the flood the dung of donkeys said to the golden apples, “We too are floating fruit,” <note>A satirical proverb mocking those who claim equality with their superiors based on proximity rather than merit.</note> so now any fool and donkey might be allowed to rail against our positions put forward here or elsewhere, in this or any other way. 

<margin>20</margin>But if there are any of such title, dignity, or competence that they are not considered unworthy of meeting with us for some reason, and to whom we might respond without disgrace to our own status, they will find a man most prompt and ready, through whom they may test the weight of their own strength.

Farewell.

<summary>In this concluding section of his preface, Giordano Bruno defends his philosophical departures from tradition, asserting that his views are grounded in reason and sensory evidence rather than dogma. He ends with a bold challenge to intellectual critics, warning that he will only engage with those of sufficient merit and dignity.</summary>

<keywords>Giordano Bruno, Pythagoras, common philosophy, Aristotelianism, reason vs faith, intellectual challenge, Thirty Seals, 16th-century philosophy</keywords>

# PHILOTHEUS

## BY GIORDANO BRUNO THE NOLAN
<note>Bruno was born in Nola, near Naples, and often used "The Nolan" as part of his title to honor his origins.</note>

### THIRTY SEALS.

You have here, most illustrious and excellent Lord, a collection
<margin>5</margin> of 30 Seals; when these are weighed in the balance, the acts of inquiry, discovery, and retention <note>original: "retentio." In the context of the Art of Memory, this refers to the ability to store and recall information.</note> may skillfully succeed.

->OF THE FIELD,<-
->which is the first Seal.<-

The Field is the first seal. It is necessary that this be
<margin>10</margin> composed of those forms <note>original: "speciebus." In Renaissance psychology, "species" were the mental images or impressions received from the senses.</note> whose likenesses are contained within the vast depth of the <term>faculty of the imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasticae facultatis." This was considered the mental workshop where sensory data was transformed into images for thought and memory.</note>, so that the sown seeds of intentions and of all imaginable things may progress toward the desired harvest. We have also willed that this [Field], so that it might be most dutifully subservient to us, should be divided into those parts
<margin>15</margin> which are perceptible, of moderate size, of neither excessive nor diminished clarity, diverse, distinct, ordered, set apart and separated by suitable intervals, [proportioned] to the height of raised human arms and the width of extended [arms], and adorned or animated with exquisite [images]...

<margin>1v</margin>
...adapted to the number of forms, should be surveyed again and again. It will be of no small benefit to you if you conceive of this field as skillfully distributed into divided portions. In this way, the <term>Talmudist</term> <note>original: "Thalmutista." A scholar of the Talmud; Bruno often drew upon Jewish mystical traditions and architectural descriptions from the Bible to create his memory palaces.</note> divided <term>Solyma</term> <note>original: "Solymam." A poetic name for Jerusalem, specifically referring here to the idealized layout of the Holy City or the Temple.</note> into four sides—the East, North, South, and West. First, he multiplied each of those
<margin>5</margin> sides by the number twelve, then subdivided them into three gates marked with the names of the Patriarchs; soon after, into twelve courtyards, each of which encompasses twelve houses; each of these houses consists of four
<margin>10</margin> rows, each of which refers to twelve chambers at most. These chambers finally receive [objects] situated either in the four corners or in the four mediating sides, creating an entrance in a certain fixed order.

## OF THE HEAVEN,

<margin>15</margin> ->which is the second Seal.<-

So that the series and order of the images of heaven may be engraved, let a sphere first be divided into four right-angled segments of the circumference by two <term>great circles</term> <note>original: "circulis magnis." In spherical geometry, a circle whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, like the equator or meridians.</note> intersecting one another. This will offer just as many distinct and equal portions, each of
<margin>20</margin> which places before the eyes a place and position for what is to be sought, found, and retained. But if you wish to cut each of the quadrants into twin parts, it will undoubtedly happen that, by multiplying the work of division, you will be less burdened in your primary purpose.
<margin>25</margin> <margin>2r</margin> Indeed, when the sphere appears delineated by three great circles intersecting | at right angles, it will provide eight equal spaces of circumferential triangles. In these triangles, you will afterwards contemplate what is positioned at the base of each, what at the peak, and what at each of the sides, through the distinctions of right, left, above, and below.

## OF THE CHAIN,
->where the third Seal is located.<-

To the seeker who proceeds by an orderly method, the "offspring"—both <term>invention</term> <note>original: "inventio." In classical rhetoric, the art of "finding" or "discovering" the arguments or ideas one wishes to use.</note> and the retention of what is discovered—is supplied by that very order. Indeed, lest any parts break away through disconnection, and so that the mastery of one thing leads directly to the mastery of the next, they shall move into interlocking <term>cycles</term> <note>original: "cyclos." Bruno uses this to describe a looping or repeating sequence that binds memories together.</note> in such a way that the "head" of a following part unfolds from the "tail" of the one preceding it. Let this be made manifest, as far as possible, in the sequence of <term>elements</term> <note>original: "elementorum." Here, Bruno is referring specifically to letters of the alphabet as the basic building blocks of his system.</note>: AB. BC. CD. DE. <margin>10</margin> EF. FG. GH. HI. IK. KL.

## OF THE TREE,
->where the fourth Seal is located.<-

If you gather simple concepts together in such a way that they sprout into branches, twigs, foliage, flowers, and fruits, <margin>15</margin> it seems to make no difference at all whether you conceive of the structure as a chain or as the trunk of a tree. Its progression and use are suggested by the coordinated elements, as you see.

# OF THE FOREST,

->where the fifth Seal is located.<-

Many trees come together to form a forest; furthermore, while this structure certainly retains the connection of its parts, it does not allow for a <term>homogeneous</term> <note>original: "homogeneam." Meaning consisting of parts all of the same kind; here, Bruno means a forest is naturally chaotic unless organized.</note> and unambiguous sequence of them, unless they are transplanted and arranged into the proper orders of distinct species: ac. cf. fg. gm. mk. kb. bd. dh. hf. fl. li. Then, in another <term>region</term> <note>original: "plaga." Literally a tract of land or climate zone; in Bruno's mnemonic system, it refers to a specific area or "room" in the memory palace.</note>, they are ordered differently: bf. fk. km. And thereafter, in a similar fashion, they shall be arranged in diverse and other regions in various ways (with the <term>chain</term> <note>original: "catena." <meta>This page continues the sequence of the "Thirty Seals," Bruno's mnemonic devices for organizing and retrieving knowledge. Having previously discussed the Chain, Tree, Forest, and Scale, he now moves to the Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Seals: the Grafter, the Farmer, and the Table.</meta>

THIRTY SEALS.

### OF THE GRAFTER,
->where the seventh Seal is located.<-

A rational and manifold cause will surely bring it about that, by looking now toward this order and now toward that, we may run through everything with everything else—here from the tree through the chain, or the chain through the tree, through the field, and through these and other things for the sake of others. Indeed, since these things succeed those, and others follow others in innumerable ways, and are arranged into a certain appearance and continued, you will be able, through your own skill, to advance through many or all of the <term>seals</term> <note>original: "sigillos." In Bruno's system, a 'seal' is a complex mental diagram or method used to organize the memory.</note> to capture what you desire.

<margin>3v</margin>
### OF THE FARMER,
->where the eighth Seal is located.<-

If a steady farmer does not abandon the field of which he is master, your expectation will hardly ever fail you. I call the "Farmer" the reasoning soul, perpetually united to its own <term>subject</term> <note>original: "subiecto." In the context of the Art of Memory, the 'subject' is the underlying foundation or "place" (locus) where mental images are stored.</note>, conducting itself in different ways according to the occasion of the various incoming forms, and capable of being turned toward the production of any species whatsoever; it provides us with an encounter that is far more lively than an <term>adjective subject</term> <note>original: "adiectivum subiectum." Likely referring to a secondary or accidental foundation rather than the primary essence of the soul's focus.</note> established elsewhere.

### OF THE TABLE,
->where the ninth Seal is located.<-

A <term>table</term> <note>original: "tabula." A grid or chart, often used in the Lullian tradition to combine letters representing different concepts.</note> used to be completed by others as well through an ordered combination of elements, while moving from the abstract to the accuser, to the adversary, to the aerial, to the afflicted, to...

### OF THE BINDER,
->where the tenth Seal is located.<-

The Binder <note>original: "Compaginator." A method for joining disparate "memory rooms" or concepts into a single sequence.</note> is he who sews together distinct fields or halls—as if they were certain separate leaves placed apart—by a certain skillful connection; he performs this effectively when he makes a farmer, or some other adjective, or any other form that was the end of one common subject, serve as the indicator for the beginning of another subject placed anywhere else (according to his wish).

<margin>20</margin> ### OF THE BANNER,
->where the eleventh Seal is located.<-

We call it a Banner <note>original: "Vexillum." This seal uses a single representative image to stand for an entire category or group of people.</note> because, according to the demand of the word or thing, you will be able to understand and assign many or few, more or fewer, to be referred to the same sign. Hence, not only one Plato, Aristotle, or Diogenes might serve you, nor just one
<margin>25</margin> Pyrrhonian, Cynic, or Epicurean <note>These refer to famous ancient Greek philosophers and their respective schools of thought.</note>, but many who are related, similar, and proportional.

THIRTY SEALS.

## ON ZEUXIS OR THE PAINTER,
->where the 12th Seal is located.<-

I have placed images bound with their own insignia and circumstances in many parts of a subject, in which the reasoning mind can write anything. **4$^v$** Thus, for me, the images of Teucer the Babylonian <note>original: "Teucri Babylonici." Teucer of Babylon was an ancient astrologer whose descriptions of the decans (zodiacal degrees) Bruno used as a massive "alphabet" for his memory system.</note> supply a reading of one hundred and three thousand propositions.

## ON PHIDIAS OR THE SCULPTOR,
->where the 13th Seal is located.<-

I have divided a common and total subject into its own proper seats <note>original: "sedes." These are the "rooms" or "places" in a memory palace.</note>, which indeed retain certain images perpetually dwelling in their own house, so that they might sound in different ways by the touch of various wanderers. There, the form coming to the subject—considered according to local and situational differences, as well as through various parts and according to various conditions—will cause the five elements to multiply through things that consist and subsist; or if it pleases to remain on the mark of a subsisting element there, it will happen that the fivefold element receives the desired formation through the signs of the other elements. <note>Phidias represents the mnemonic method of carving out "spaces" or "seats" for information, where letters or basic units (elements) can be combined and transformed.</note>

## ON DAEDALUS,
->or the 14th Seal.<-

What Phidias performed in words, let Daedalus <note>The mythical architect and inventor; here representing the use of mental "tools" or mechanical instruments to organize memory.</note> practice in intentions and through things noted by intentions. Therefore, I have established many instruments and tools, with which, in which, through...

### XV. The Seal.

I looked upon five <note>Though Bruno mentions five "atria" (halls), he proceeds to describe a sequence of seven distinct stages of character construction.</note> halls: from the first came a
man; in the second, he chose one of many items

multipartite and varied combinations (and even

## ON THE NUMERATOR,
<margin>20</margin> ### which is the XVI. Seal.

Among all things, what better than Number shall supply
all things? Not only is everything derived from it, but
it is itself the very mode of understanding; it includes all
proportional things; one may contemplate it in all things
and all things in it. For Pythagoras, this is a
certain substance and the primary archetype of things; <margin>5^v</margin>
at present, it serves not only as a method for the order
of things to be conceived and retained, but also
(if it be fashioned into something imaginable) as the

### THIRTY SEALS.

<sig>6r</sig>

...will be able to present the numbered forms of ordered things. Therefore, let the practitioner take up a different material for each distinct decade <note>original: "decadum". In Bruno’s system, a "decade" represents the "tens" place (10, 20, 30, etc.).</note>, so that the first decade is assigned **linen**, the second **wool**, the third **leather**, the fourth **wood**, the fifth **stone**, the sixth **crystal**, <margin>5</margin> the seventh **iron**, the eighth **bronze**, the ninth **silver**, and the tenth **gold**. Let him also take up different forms (representing the different digits within the decades) so that:
- a **column** signifies one, 
- a **portico** signifies two, 
- a **tripod** signifies three, 
- a **chest** signifies four, 
- a **seat** signifies five, 
- a **table** signifies six, 
- an **altar** signifies seven, 
<margin>10</margin> - a **bed** signifies eight, 
- a **gallows** signifies nine, 
- and a **tree** signifies ten. 

In the same and similar fashion, by diversifying with many other materials and forms, you will be able to extend these numbered subjects for yourself into infinity.

## ON THE CENTURION,

<margin>20</margin> -> which is the XVII. Seal. <-

The people of **Nola** <note>original: "Nolani". Bruno's home town.</note> forged for me the first century <note>original: "centuriam". A group of 100 mnemonic slots.</note>; the **Neapolitans** <note>original: "Parthenopaei".</note> the second; the **Capuans** the third; and the **Salernitans** the fourth. Within these, I conceived that there should gather:
- in the first decade of each century, **friends** who have been perceived;
- in the second, **brothers**, whether imagined or real;
<margin>25</margin> - in the third, **counselors**;
- in the fourth, **servants**;
- in the fifth, **boys**;
- in the sixth, **pilots**;
- in the seventh, **teachers**;
- in the eighth, **preachers**;
- in the ninth, **adversaries**;
- and in the tenth, **schoolmates**. 

Such is the significance of things for me—

## ON THE ENCYCLOPEDIC SQUARE.
<note>original: "De Quadrato Encyclio". "Encyclio" refers to a general or "all-encompassing" system of knowledge, often visualized as a circle or, in this case, a square.</note>

Whenever four stars of the first magnitude <note>In astronomy, "magnitude" refers to brightness; here, Bruno uses it to denote the "rank" or "size" of a category within his memory system.</note> have four others of the second magnitude placed at their sides,

### ON THE COMPOSITE AND THE ELEMENT.
<margin>10</margin> <margin>r</margin> #### XX. Seal.

An epigram or an ode used to bring back to my mind a group of ten <note>original: "denarium," referring to a set of ten mnemonic items or perhaps a mental "coin" of memory.</note> already counted out. The work itself, once distinguished into its own proper parts, first suggested books of sections, then the chapters of the books, and immediately thereafter the portions of the chapters. This continued while the universal and general matter provided me with reasoned discourses, <margin>15</margin> and these in turn brought forth their own propositions and sentences. From these, what could have prevented an approach toward simple, indivisible terms? <note>Bruno is describing a "top-down" memory technique: breaking a large work into chapters, then sentences, then individual words or "elements."</note> Thus, **I HATE** of the first, **THE PROFANE** of the second, **CROWD** of the third, **AND I KEEP THEM AWAY** of the fourth <note>original: "ODI... PROFANVM... VULGVS... ET ARCEO." This is the famous opening line of Horace’s Odes (III.1).</note> revealed the intent of the chapter in its very third division. <margin>20</margin> Indeed, when the meanings of the elements—or the primary compositions made from them—were fitted to these signs of intent, an extremely easy path was opened for the mind to reach the parts of those very intentions. For example, by the expressed sign of Hatred <note>original: "Odii," referring to the word "Odi" (I hate).</note>, the worker signified by **O** would have hated, and the teacher <note>original: "didascalus," from the Greek word for instructor.</note> signified by **D** would have hated, and by **I**...
<note>Bruno is using the letters of the word "ODI" as "pegs" to store information: O for *Operarius* (Worker), D for *Didascalus* (Teacher), etc.</note>

5      In this matter, an urgent necessity occasionally made me resourceful, so that I might either allow <term>elements</term><note>The basic building blocks of Bruno’s memory system, often represented by single letters or phonemes.</note> to pass into and be expanded into <term>composites</term><note>Complex images or words formed by joining multiple "elements."</note>, or permit these composites to be touched upon and contracted into those elements. For thus a parchment that is insufficient for the intended writing requires another to be joined to it, or, if it is too spacious, requires itself to be narrowed <margin>η v</margin>
10 and shortened even more.
      I would sometimes arrange the multiplication of forms for myself in this way: since an element or a combination had once signified a person set before me, I would immediately afterward seek out the result—either through that same person marked in various ways, or better, through another agent of the same name, or a woman, or a beast, or some inanimate object (which had been arranged to represent and signify the same element).
      At this point, when things were being connected to things, lest the limbs coalesce as if into a confused mass of a body, I established more prominent headings by illuminating and marking each with numbers—as if among military cohorts—which might more effectively report not only their own order but also that of those belonging to them.

<header>THIRTY SEALS</header>

...with a thousand fathers or headings, along with their children, bodies, and distinct limbs, you should prepare in advance a hundred living subjects <note>In Bruno’s system, "living subjects" are active mnemonic images—usually people or mythological figures—who "act out" information to make it memorable.</note> arranged in a specific order from the aforementioned series, in which the matter being treated is understood. These subjects, running through the numbers of the numerator or any other series, will distribute the headings into limbs,
<margin>8r</margin>
and the limbs into their own specific joints. For what of it? If, from a hundred men, each one in succession passes through a hundred different beds <note>Bruno uses "beds" (*cubilia*) as a metaphor for *loci*, the fixed locations in a "memory palace" where images are placed.</note>, will they not lay out ten thousand intentions for you? If you wish to double these, you can do so simply by adding as many beds or by multiplying the men. Is it not also possible within these—just as materials are subordinate to other materials—to subject men to men (as servants, friends, or successors) or houses to houses and halls to halls by similar relationships? Will not these last perceived things, being subjected to various circumstances in a certain order, provide you with far richer material for inquiry, discovery, and retention?

### ON THE EMPIRICAL.
### XXIII. The Seal.

I assigned various workers to various houses—those houses, I say, in which gardens, granaries, storehouses <note>original: "apothecae"</note>, heated rooms <note>original: "hypocausta"—referring to the Roman system of underfloor heating, used here as a specific room type in a memory palace.</note>, and kitchens were found; in which vegetables, crops, seasonings, baths, food, and drink were prepared. Here, even in a narrower space as the requirements of the matter demanded, the things necessary for each and relevant to each appeared more readily. Yet this was not done without the foresight of a studious skill, so that the proportion of number and measure for each thing should by no means be ignored. There, indeed, apart from the houses, stood a courtyard, where "ill-counseling hunger and base poverty, grief and avenging cares have placed their beds" <note>original: "malesuada fames et turpis egestas, luctus et ultrices posuere cubilia curae." ## ON THE DICE <note>original: "DE ALEA"</note>
### XXIV. The Seal.

Since there is no vacant space for the "dice" <note>Bruno uses the game of chance as a metaphor for the random or unpredictable associations that can occur in memory</note> in the Empirical, the Fountain, the Mirror, the Potter, and the others, nor in the field, nor in the sky, nor in the general circles of knowledge <note>original: "encycliis"</note> and the rest, we have devised these further things. All these figures, equipped with other functions, would affect the throwers in the subsequent encounters. Next, different dining rooms <note>original: "triclinia"—referring to the three-sided couches used in Roman dining rooms, here acting as complex memory locations</note> were destined for different conflicts, each of which contained four living subjects. From the accidents of these subjects, they would signify the throws of the four players: while in their turns this king places his scepter, the old man lies down, death reaps, and the queen is embraced. There and elsewhere, the queen, death, the old man, the king, and the others arrive similarly and yet differently. ### ON THE HEAVENS,
->which is the XXV Seal.<-

<margin>10</margin> There was a figure of worldly eternity, a type of the revolving earth, a mark of two principles opposing each other back and forth, and many other outlines and descriptions of complex intentions. When I had inspected each of these, I referred them into a field, or a commander <note>original: "centurionem," used here as a mnemonic placeholder</note>, or some other <margin>15</margin> thing in which they might be set against the spears of opponents aiming at them—spears by no means to be lost. Therefore, set against the rotation of the earth was the line: "In the meantime, rising Dawn left the Ocean" <note>original: "Oceanum interea surgens aurora reliquit"; Virgil, Aeneid 4.129. Bruno uses this verse to represent the movement of the world</note>; fighting against the immortality of the soul was: "The shepherd Corydon burned for the beautiful Alexis" <note>original: "Formosum pastor Corydon ardebat Alexin"; Virgil, Eclogues 2.1. Bruno interprets these literary figures as symbols of physical corruption or desire</note>. In the first verse, <margin>20</margin> they referred "Ocean" to magnitude, "In the meantime" to natural faculty, "Rising" to the lunar symbol, "Dawn" to a sail-bearing and oared ship <note>original: "veligerae remitaeque ratis"; Bruno's text contains a non-standard spelling here</note>, and "Left" to the medium of lack. In the second verse, I conceived "Beautiful" as the unstable and <margin>10r</margin> continuously variable; "Shepherd" <margin>25</margin> presented itself to me as something dissoluble; "Corydon" was present as a specimen enslaved to the body; "Burned" expressed the clash of opposites; and "Alexis" represented passive matter—

## ON THE CIRCEAN FIELDS, GARDENS, AND CAVES.
<note>Circe was the enchantress from the Odyssey; Bruno uses "Circean" to refer to the transformative power of the imagination.</note>

### XXVI. Seal.

<margin>15</margin> A mental image, when seen alongside its surrounding shape and form, easily presents itself to our inner sense. We can very easily either assign a specific location to certain images, or attach certain images to locations in such a way that, when needed, the logic of that quality may come forward, designated by its relationship to that specific place. <margin>20</margin> Hence it happens that we find the natural faculty is greatly relieved from heavier work by using numbers fashioned into sensible images, which are assigned to many places according to the plurality of those images. | <margin>10^v</margin> For example, if on the Wheel, which they call the Wheel of Fortune, <margin>25</margin> Italians are assigned to the number ten <note>original: "denarium"</note>, Gauls to the number twenty <note>original: "vigenarium"</note>, and Spaniards to the number thirty <note>original: "trigenarium"</note>, their specific members would be distinguished by certain signs or actions within those groups of ten.

## ON THE PILGRIM,
### which is the XXVII. Seal.

I have sometimes established ten common subjects <note>original: "subiecta," referring to the underlying mental "places" or containers used in a memory palace</note> shaped with powerful variety, each of which would encompass twenty-four or more or fewer partial components. The intent was that the pilgrim <note>original: "peregrinus"; Bruno often uses the figure of a traveler or pilgrim to represent the active mind moving through the rooms of a memory palace.</note>—who is the first to explore these areas—would so conduct himself and be affected by the tools <note>original: "utensilibus"</note> he encounters, that [he might lead] me toward the [knowledge] of some first order or [contem-]<margin>20</margin>

[...contem-]plation, or inquiry, or habit. <margin>5</margin>For this reason, Aristotle will be affected by the subjects <note>original: "subiecta," the places or images used in a memory system</note> differently than Plato would be, and he will express different things either by himself or through a companion. If indeed you require even smaller particles of parts, then subordinate house to house, field to field, theater to theater;

## ON THE KABBALISTIC CLOISTER AND TEMPLE.
### XXVIII. The Seal.

You have twenty-two cloisters and temples, in place of the twenty-two elements <note>original: "elementorum," referring to the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet, which in Kabbalistic tradition are the "elements" or building blocks of creation</note>, each of which contains 22 seats. 
<margin>5</margin> These seats receive and provide the same items in the same order as the elements did; from these, if one proceeds to the 22 arts and the 22 gestures of each individual art, the powers of three or four radicals <note>original: "radicalium," likely referring to the root letters or fundamental principles in a mnemonic or linguistic system</note> will lie hidden <note>The original Latin text has a typo: "delitesceut" for "delitescent."</note>.

# ON THE COMBINER,
->which is the 29th Seal.<-

Three types of combinations are proposed here. The first has a consistent element that precedes another <margin>5</margin> persistent element; the second follows the opposite order; the third is one in which another persistent middle element—either "liquid" or "non-liquid" <note>Bruno uses "liquid" to refer to the letters L, R, and N, which in phonetics and his memory system can easily blend with other consonants to form more complex sounds and images.</note>—is received between the antecedent and the consequent. No difficulty appears in the formation of the first and second types, but in the third we have established it such that, <margin>10</margin> by a fivefold difference of position, a fivefold persistent medium is captured in the following combinatorial.

Bb. bc. bd. be. bf. bg. bi. bk. bl. bm. bn. bns. bnt.
bp. br. bs. bt. bv. bx.

Cb. cc. cd. ce. cf. cg. ci. cl. cm. cn. cns. cnt. co. cp.
<margin>15</margin> cr. cs. ct. cv. cx.

A similar judgment applies to the other elements to be combined; we have also seen fit to provide for a fivefold difference of the work's location in the operation, just as in the first combinatorial a triple difference suggested the "liquefaction" of L, R, and N.

<margin>20</margin> The combinatorial of the first kind was completed using 22 imagined "brothers," to whom a fivefold arriving difference brought forth a concomitant element. The combinatorial of the second kind was noted according to the second element of the combination in 5 imagined "friends" affected by 22 qualities <margin>25</margin> or circumstances. In the third kind, let the first order be of the bound; 2. of the sick; 3. of the lame; 4. of the blind; 5. of the bearded; 6. of the marked <note>original: "signatis," likely referring to people with distinctive scars, brands, or physical signs used as memory markers.</note>; 7. of the dark; 8. of the white; 9. of the livid; 10. of the clean; 11. of the celibate; 12. of the rivals; 13. | of the dutiful; 14. of the glorious, by which a sign is held.

### CHAPTER IV. ON THE MULTIPLICATION OF RULES.

## Section I.

<margin>g 1^r</margin>You will be able to understand the multiplication of <term>rules</term><note>In Bruno’s system, "rules" are logical categories or tools—often derived from the Lullist tradition—used to frame questions about the nature of reality.</note> sufficiently by yourself from what has been discussed above; nevertheless, for the sake of clarity in teaching, let us not be reluctant to list the proposed methods. 

Rules are multiplied, first, through the "breadth" of their meaning—because they do not seek answers within the narrow scope of any single defined science. Second, they are multiplied through their listed types. Third, they are multiplied through their "complication" <note>Bruno uses "complication" in the literal Latin sense of *complicatio*, meaning a "folding together" or interweaving of concepts.</note> with one another, where "whether" is joined with "what." For example, one might ask: *What is this thing that you say exists? Is it the very thing you are defining? Regarding what is this thing so defined?* 

This is done by leading each rule through every other rule, just as lines are drawn from one point on the edge of a circle to all other designated points. Finally, one rule may be led through two others, or two through one, as shown in that same figure. There, one of the questions (designated here by the letter **A** and placed in the center) is led first to individual points and then from those individuals to all others. For instance: 
**BF**: *Is it such as you say?* <note>original: "utrum est tale quale dicis?"</note> 
**CKB**: *What is that thing, with which something else exists at some time?* <note>original: "quid est illud, cum quo aliquid est aliquando?"</note>

<summary>Bruno explains how his logical rules can be multiplied and combined using geometric diagrams, specifically introducing the 'Seal of Heaven' as a tool for interweaving different categories of inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>Giordano Bruno, Art of Memory, multiplication of rules, Seal of Heaven, combinatorics, mnemonics, logic, Caelum</keywords>

# FIGURE OF THE SEAL OF SEALS

->for the derivation and multiplication of subjects and forms.<-
<note>original: "pro deductione et multiplicatione subiectorum et formarum." In Bruno’s mnemonic system, "derivation" refers to the process of drawing specific ideas out of general categories, while "multiplication" refers to the combinatorial power of the system to generate an infinite variety of thoughts and associations by connecting different points of data.</note>

<image-desc>The page features two circular geometric diagrams related to the mnemonic and philosophical systems of Giordano Bruno. 

The primary diagram at the top is a large circle with twelve points marked around its circumference, labeled with the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, and M (omitting J). Each letter is oriented outward from the center. Every point is connected to every other point on the circle by a straight line, creating a complex web of intersections that forms a "complete graph" in geometric terms. This dense network of lines creates various concentric polygons and star patterns within the circle. This represents the <term>universal connection: the idea that every concept in the universe is potentially linked to every other concept</term>.

The secondary diagram below is smaller. It features the same twelve labeled points (A through M) around its circumference. In this figure, lines are only drawn radiating from the top point (A) to each of the other eleven points on the circle, creating a fan-like or shell-like appearance within the lower half of the circle. This illustrates a <term>linear derivation: how a single "subject" (A) can be applied to many different "forms" or categories (B through M)</term>.</image-desc>

<note>These diagrams are not merely mathematical; they are intended to be visualized by the student of memory. By "placing" information at these lettered points, the practitioner can mentally "walk" along the lines to retrieve related ideas. The complexity of the top circle reflects the "multiplicity" of the universe, while the lower circle shows the "deduction" or unfolding of a single principle.</note>

### THE ALPHABETICAL CORRESPONDENCE OF THE SEAL

In Bruno's system, this represents the harmony and mirroring of all concepts within the mind.</note>

## EXPLANATION OF THE THIRTY SEALS.

Setting aside all superstitious concern for words, the thirty seals which we have arranged are opened to you by us—much like those who unroll and untie a tangled and implicit thread, or who lead forth and unfold a hidden and folded cloth.

->Explanation of the first seal.<-

The **Field** was the first seal <note>The "Field" (Campus) refers to the mental space or "canvas" upon which a practitioner of the Art of Memory arranges their images.</note>, which must be prepared first as the subject of the entire work and artifice. This is the "place" which is distinguished in the second part of the theory of the *Art of Memory* <note>original: *Artis reminiscendi*</note> through the differences between common and proper <margin>5</margin> characteristics, and is distributed into all its various species.

In this context, we have preferred to say that "likenesses of places" are sought, rather than "places" themselves. For we have found that when these are presented to the external eyes, they move the mind less by their physical presence <margin>10</margin> than when they are surveyed by the internal eyes of the <term>phantastic faculty<gloss>The power of the mind to form, retain, and manipulate mental images; the imagination.</gloss></term>. This most ample bay is titled **Phantasia** (Imagination) because what it has received—already finished and determined—from the external senses, <margin>15</margin> it then... <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence.</note>

...is [continued]. For concerning whatever subject we wish to speak, <margin>a 3^r</margin> whether gathering from the discoveries of others or reaping from our own meditations, we do so in such a way that, looking upon the subject itself as if it were a tree, we first consider its **roots**—namely, the original principles, <margin>5</margin> causes, and elements; then the **trunk**—that is, its own essence and being; next the **branches**—that is, the powers, faculties, and virtues; then the **leaves**, namely the proper accidents <term>accidents (accidentia): in philosophy, these are qualities or characteristics that a thing has but which are not essential to its nature (e.g., the color of a shirt is an accident, whereas being a garment is its essence).</term> and circumstances; then the **flowers**, such as actions and operations; and finally the **fruits**, which are the acts and <margin>10</margin> works. We do this so that, by this method, the order (by which we arrange the material) provides for invention, judgment, and retention <term>invention, judgment, and retention: three of the five traditional "canons" of rhetoric; invention is finding arguments, judgment (or disposition) is organizing them, and retention is memory.</term>.

For those proceeding analytically as well, let a "tree of demonstrable matter" be established. For its **roots**, let the senses, imagination, persuasion, authority, and other things of that kind which stir up belief <margin>15</margin> be held; for its **twin trunk**, let there be the investigation of verification—one on the part of the subject, the other on the part of the predicate; and for the **complex** formed in the convergence of the twin trunk, it holds the entire union of subject and predicate. If indeed it is asked whether matter exists in <margin>20</margin> actuality, one must inspect the reasons on the side of the matter, then the reasons on the side of the act, and the reasons for these same things on the side of the matter’s own actuality. In proportion to the multitude of branches, it admits a multitude of **middle terms** <term>middle terms (media): the linking concepts in a logical syllogism that connect the subject to the predicate.</term>, whereby some are referred to one part of the trunk, <margin>523</margin> others to the other part, and others to the trunk as a whole. It <margin>25</margin> also takes as **fruits** those things which follow from those granted middle terms. For the **bystanders** and those standing around, it receives a diverse and multi-faceted crowd, <margin>a 3^v</margin> regarding which some are watchful, some rest, some doubt, some decide, some neigh, others grunt <note>original: "hinniunt... grunniunt." Bruno frequently used animal sounds to satirize the different ways scholars or critics reacted to his philosophical ideas.</note>, while others [stay] under the shade of that tree...

<note>original: "Tityre... Tu... Patulae... Recubans... Sub... Tegmine... Fagi." These lines are a mnemonic device. The first word of each line, when read in sequence, reconstructs the famous opening line of Virgil’s first Eclogue: "Tityre, tu patulae recubans sub tegmine fagi" (Tityrus, you reclining under the cover of a spreading beech tree). Bruno is demonstrating how a "tree" of information can be condensed into a single recognizable structure.</note>

—the other method is that by which we find <term>discovery: "inventio," the rhetorical art of finding and developing arguments</term> and <term>judgment: "iudicium," the ability to evaluate the validity of those arguments</term> to be amplified. This occurs when we investigate that "universal" quality—which we have considered in all parts and circumstances of the tree—within the individual things said about it, within the thing itself, and within the things that exist <margin>15</margin> around it. Furthermore, the "Tree" is expanded into a "Forest" <note>original: "sylva." In classical rhetoric, a "sylva" refers to a raw collection of materials or a dense thicket of ideas yet to be organized.</note> through the manifold forms of discovery, a dilatation that is discussed in another place.

### Explanation of the Ladder, which is the sixth seal.

Discovery and judgment are tested through the "Ladder," whenever an <margin>20</margin> ascent occurs from lower things to higher things. This is because those things said of the lower according to their worth are verified in the higher things by a greater and more eminent reason. Even if these same predicates cannot belong to the higher things formally <note>To belong "formally" means the object possesses the literal characteristic (e.g., a human is formally "rational"). To belong "effectively" or "eminently" means the cause possesses the power of that quality in a higher, more perfect way (e.g., God is not "rational" in a human sense but is the source of all Reason).</note>, they are nevertheless ascribed to them as effective principles <margin>25</margin> to be named by a more sublime logic. Those things, however, which in higher things [are found] by the dignity of the first...

<summary>Bruno illustrates the "Forest" seal using a mnemonic verse based on Virgil and introduces the "Ladder" seal, which explains how to understand higher truths by observing their reflections in lower, material things.</summary>

->Explanation of the **Farmer**, which is the eighth seal.<-

We establish someone as perpetually present in the **Field** <note>original: "Campo." In Bruno's system, the "Field" is the mental space or "memory palace" where the practitioner places mnemonic images.</note>, whom we call sometimes an "adjective subject," sometimes the "soul of the place," but now indeed the **Farmer**. We spoke of this in the second part of the theory of the *Art of Remembering*, when we brought the final condition of subjects into consideration; however, what we introduce here under the name of the "farmer" differs from what we called the "adjective of the place" there. This is because what we command to be placed here is animate, and such a living being that—whether by existing within, inhering, assisting, or surrounding—it can be receptive to all things and consequently capable of representing them. Hence, just as they called the world the image of God, so they called man the image of the world.

This was the starting principle by which I was moved toward achieving the methods of the art of memory. I was able to fish it out, even as a boy, from the works <note>original: "monimentis." ->Explanation of the **Painter**, which is the twelfth seal.<-

"Painters and poets have always had an equal power of daring whatever they like" <note>A famous quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*. Bruno uses it to justify the creative and imaginative nature of his mnemonic and philosophical system.</note>. The first and most excellent painter is the **imaginative faculty** <term>phantastica virtus: The power of the mind to create and manipulate mental images (phantasms), which Bruno considers the foundation of all thought.</term>; the first and most excellent poet is a certain enthusiasm—either innate or newly inspired—arising from the impulse of the **thinking faculty**, by which they are stirred by a divine or similar inspiration to present something appropriately devised. The principle for both is the same; therefore, philosophers are in a way painters and poets, <margin>a 8^r</margin> poets are painters and philosophers, and painters are philosophers and poets. Consequently, true poets, true painters, and true philosophers love and admire one another. One is not a painter unless he fashions and meditates in some way; and without a certain meditation and painting, a poet...

### EXPLANATION OF THE THIRTY SEALS
<sig>18</sig>

...one will be able to conceive all things from all things. I mean "to conceive" either by the mode of identity—if they are of the same genus, species, or number—or by similarity, where a representable thing is linked to its correlative. Or one might use proportion, if they are proportional; or even irony, <margin>5</margin> if they are discordant. An example of the latter is when authors speak of the "riches of punishments" and "the treasures of wrath" <note>original: "poenarum divitias" and "thesauros irae." Bruno is noting how words for positive things like wealth are used ironically to describe the intensity of divine judgment.</note>. This is a mental invention that occurs with a certain elegance, even though "riches" and "treasures" are usually reserved for desirable things. 

We can similarly relate a representable thing to its correlative through other types of opposition; <margin>b 2<sup>r</sup></margin> for **Man** and the **World** are opposed <margin>10</margin> as the container and the contained, or as the great and the small <note>This refers to the common Renaissance idea of the Microcosm (Man) and the Macrocosm (the Universe).</note>. Through these many other types of opposition, man can be described as a resident of the world, a wanderer, a small thing, a spectator, a mortal, and so on. 

Likewise, someone who compares **Justice** to a lamp modifies the image to convey its character and essence. By considering the differences [between a real lamp and the concept], <margin>15</margin> he is led to call it such a lamp that is never consumed or extinguished by any passage of time. If one represents **Temperance** as a woman, he should describe her brow as one that no wrinkle of old age has ever furrowed, and her skin as something that no amount of time could wither. 

Through exaggeration <margin>20</margin> and a specific kind of representation, many things are also adapted to their comparisons. This is why, when Job wished to describe "fate" <note>Bruno is interpreting the permanence of Job's words as a description of fate or destiny.</note> through the image of a book, he realized a normal book was not enough to signify the concept. He called it a book that records the future on a lead plate with an iron stylus, or carved into flint and stone, <margin>25</margin> or even on engraved diamond <note>original: "plumbi lamina, stilo ferreo, in celte et silice... adamante." This refers to Job 19:24, where Job wishes his words were permanently engraved.</note>. 

Conversely, when an image provides more information than is necessary for the subject at hand, we use a kind of "subtraction" or "contraction" to make the similarity fit. In all these matters, finally, one must focus on the point where the...

### Explanation of the Daedalus, which is the fourteenth seal.

Just as every craftsman who intends to produce many different effects proceeds to his work either with many tools or with a single instrument manipulated in various and multifaceted ways, so it is with this Daedalus. <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus was the master architect and inventor who designed the Labyrinth; here, Bruno uses him as a symbol for a "universal tool" of the mind.</note> His subject matter can be manifold and of many kinds; indeed, he is confident that he can operate upon all things in his proper order. He prepares himself to pursue the intended work through various means according to the variety of things: at times through the sensible **Field**, at times through the **Chain**, at times through the **Tree**, at times through the **Numberer**...

### Explanation of the Centurion, which is the seventeenth seal.

<margin>5</margin>For laying the foundations and preparing the primary mediated parts—as well as the immediate neighboring parts—of general concepts, common subjects, or applicable forms intended for <term>invention</term> <note>original: *inventionem*; the rhetorical art of finding arguments or ideas</note> or for <term>retention</term> <note>original: *retentionem*; the art of memory</note>, it is difficult to find a better or even a similar device. <margin>10</margin>By this art, we will immediately and firmly possess knowledge of many things (which we cannot easily or briefly retain by natural ability or other artificial means), such as: what a thing is, how great it is, its place in a series, its quantity, where it is located, and how each thing relates to others. By this reasoning, the <term>Arithmetician</term> or the <term>Number-Counter</term> <note>original: *Arithmetricus seu Numerator*; referring to the sixteenth seal</note> (which is the seal mentioned just previously) is enriched. <margin>15</margin>For from ordered "homelands" <note>original: *patriis*; in Bruno's system, these are primary memory locations or categories</note> you obtain ordered groups of hundreds; from the various conditions of men subordinated to those homelands, you will have subordinated groups of tens (decades), which in a similar manner take up single-digit numbers. Finally, once many numbers are completed, you may use these individuals to pursue the tasks of either discovering or remembering information. <margin>20</margin>

### Explanation of the Encyclic Square, which is the eighteenth seal.

We have a twofold primary and general method through which one inquires into and discovers things arranged in an orderly fashion; this method is especially <margin>25</margin>suited for representing and retaining those things that have been arranged. **536**

# GIORDANO BRUNO

<page-num>142</page-num>

The first of these is by the square on a plane, which is the cube in solid form; the second is by the circle on a plane, which is the sphere in solid form. For in these mathematical figures, **encyclic** <note>original: *encyclia*; from the Greek *enkyklios*, meaning "circular" or "general," here referring to a structured, comprehensive mnemonic device</note> proportions can be taken in a twofold way: namely, according to either a single dimension or a triple difference of dimension.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, the **encyclical square** is produced when four <term>intentions</term> <note>original: *intentiones*; in Bruno's logic, these are mental concepts or "points of focus" directed toward an object</note> are formed upon a single subject; and above each of these four intentions (which now take the place of the subject), four others are formed, each of which is again subjected to four subsequent intentions. One continues in this manner step by step, as far as the intention of the one arranging and the requirements of the matter to be arranged will permit.

->*Explanation of the Circular Encyclic, which is the nineteenth seal.*<-

<margin>b 5r</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In almost the same sequence and proportion in the circular as in the square encyclic, the apposition <note>the act of placing things side-by-side or applying one concept to another</note> of things to things is proposed to be carried out. Furthermore, just as the circle and the sphere, or the square and the cube, are referred to different—though at least proximate—principles, and as the measurements of both types differ; so we establish different encyclia for them. Of these, one is used for the discovery of distinctions and divisions within the same thing; the other, however, is for the discovery of the multiples <note>complex relationships or varied aspects</note> which exist and are produced around that same thing. The apposition of the circular encyclic may be made manifest in a quadrant of a circle, which is easily visualized.

-> Explanation of the Composite and the Element, which is the twentieth seal. <-

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This seal is what we understood by the name of "verbal places" <note>original: *verbalium locorum*; a mnemonic technique where specific words, rather than images or locations, serve as the "seats" for storing information</note>, and it is suited not only for the retention of memory, but also in no small measure for <term>invention</term> <note>the rhetorical art of "finding" or "discovering" arguments and ideas for a speech</note>.

<margin>5</margin>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Indeed, it is used for memorization, as when we arrange the parts and sentences of a speech in an orderly fashion within "composites"—that is, in the words themselves. | For example, we might let the first <margin>537</margin> word represent someone "hating" or "detested" <note>original: *odiens vel exosus*</note>, whom we have actually known or have imagined to be so; the second, someone

We shall present the remaining parts in order, through the other words following in sequence.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It also contributes to invention, since from all words we can recall all <term>intentions</term> <note>original: *intentiones*; mental concepts or directions of thought</note>, and from all and any <margin>b 5v</margin> intentions, all other intentions are awakened and arise.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This method is not useful for all species of <term>invention</term> <note>the process of discovering arguments or ideas</note>, but only for those that produce persuasion. However, so that it may be able to contribute to invention in a universal sense, it must be provided for in this way: that these terms are not taken as mere forms, but rather as the subjects of forms. Thus, in the "hater" <note>original: *osore*</note> we find something that signifies **essence**; in the "profane" <note>original: *profano*</note>, **power**; in the "common" <note>original: *vulgato*</note>, **operation**; and in the "warder-off" <note>original: *arcente*</note>, we refer to **circumstances**. 

<margin>15</margin>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In this way, for the work of invention, we first inquire into what has been said, what should be said, and what can be said regarding the essence and being of the proposed matter. Second, what can be said regarding its habits, dispositions, faculties, and its passive and active principles. Third, what can be said regarding the effects and operations by which the thing exists and those which flow from it. Fourth, how it exists, and with what concurrent and co-causing factors; and so on for the rest through the remaining parts.

<margin>20</margin>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Accordingly, just as a speech is resolved into words as its most immediate parts, and into syllables and elements <note>original: *elementa*; here meaning the letters of the alphabet</note> as its more remote and primary parts, so too are the general signs of inventions resolved into particular and individual ones. 

<margin>25</margin>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For elements have things which they represent, and they have things by which they are represented; for the letter **A** represents many "Aristotles" and "Aristarchuses" <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famous grammarian; Bruno uses him and Aristotle as standard examples for names starting with 'A'</note>, and many Aristarchuses and many Aristotles are represented by the letter **A**. And so, both through the order of individuals signified by the elements, and through the combinations of those elements presented, and through those things denoted by whole [words]...

### Explanation of the Wheel, which is the twenty-first seal.

The subject of the **Wheel** is compared to an atrium <note>a central hall or courtyard</note>; the shaper is compared to a potter; and the "formable intention" <note>original: *intentio formabilis*; the mental concept or raw data to be shaped by the mind</note> is compared to the clay. Therefore, let there be in the Wheel, or atrium A, twelve, twenty-four, or thirty <margin>10</margin> **workshops** <note>original: *officinae*; mnemonic "places" or stations where specific types of activity occur</note>. For example:
1. a bird-catcher’s,
2. a physician’s,
3. a soldier’s,
4. a cup-bearer’s,
5. a musician’s,
6. a writer’s,
7. a farmer’s,
8. a shoemaker’s,
9. a priest’s,
10. a <term>fuller’s</term> <note>original: *fullonis*; a person who cleans and thickens raw cloth</note>,
11. a barber’s,
<margin>15</margin> 12. a reader’s.
If a single person—whether acting, cooperating, or receiving an action—is moved through these workshops and their various circumstances, they will provide at least twelve intentions. If there are two people, they provide at least twenty-four; if three, they will provide at least thirty-six.

If you wish to practice this method in **mathematics** <note>original: *mathematicis*; in Bruno's era, this often referred specifically to astrology and astronomy</note>—for example, <margin>20</margin> if you wish to remember the aspects of the stars regarding their significance <margin>539</margin> and the placements of the planets within the zodiac signs—you can prepare the twelve **houses** <note>astrological divisions of the sky</note> shaped by their circumstances. You can set them up so that their parts and members contain exactly those things most suitable for the individual considerations to be made about them and within them. ## Concerning the Empirical <note>original: *De Empirico*; referring to an experimental or practical approach, often associated with medicine in this period</note>, which is the twenty-third seal.

This seal is more obvious than to require any explanation. Through these gardens and courtyards, many sick people can follow in their own orders; these diverse individuals will be able to form various memorable intentions <note>mental concepts or specific bits of information</note> and complete the required remedies, while they themselves—or those chosen to represent them—are affected in some way either by the objects or toward the objects that are necessary and useful to them.

## Concerning the Dice <note>original: *De Alea*</note>, which is the twenty-fourth seal.

Through all the methods of figuring and presenting that have preceded and those that follow, we could not have provided for the memory of dice <note>referring to the difficulty of memorizing random combinations or sequences in games of chance</note> and a similar order of things to be retained. For that reason, we have devised this particular and specific path, which is too clearly explained to require further words.

## Explanation of the Gorgias <note>Gorgias of Leontini was a famous Greek Sophist and rhetorician; Bruno names this seal after him to signify its use in formal debate and rhetoric.</note>, which is the twenty-fifth seal.

For arguments of various kinds pertaining to different theses and subjects of debate—which might otherwise present an image of tangled confusion and chaotic disorder between what is being defended and those who are attacking—<margin>5</margin> let these elements be referred to specific and well-defined "places" <note>original: *loca*; the 'seats' or 'loci' used in a memory palace to anchor information</note> arranged in the sequence we have introduced here.

Therefore, let common "places" <note>original: *communia loca*; general rhetorical headings or categories</note> pre-arranged according to the diversity of axioms, positions, and problems, receive and return specific objections based on the number of particular "places." <margin>541</margin>
<margin>10</margin> This "Gorgias" (for thus we have chosen to name the Disputant <note>original: *Disputatorem*; the person engaged in formal debate</note>, whom this seal primarily serves) will be able to apply himself to his proper functions not only in matters of positive word-choice <note>original: *verbalibus positivis*</note>, but also in all other types of mnemonic locations. For chambers <note>original: *cubilia*; literally 'beds' or 'resting places,' here meaning specific spots in the memory architecture</note> arranged in different ways, <margin>15</margin> numbers fashioned in various forms, and diverse underlying chains of connection <note>original: *concatenationes*</note> will serve the quantity and variety of proofs to be debated.

Since the conclusion is already known in these instances, and consequently two of the three terms of the argument are known, it will be sufficient to have placed only the image <note>original: *figuram*; a mental picture or symbol</note> of the middle term <note>original: *medii*; in formal logic, the term that connects the subject and predicate in a syllogism</note>.

### Explanation of the Combiner, which is the twenty-ninth seal.

This Combiner teaches how to very conveniently represent a multitude of infinite, differing syllables using a very few images. It proposes three combinatory arrangements to be established: <margin>5</margin> the first in which a consonant precedes a vowel <note>original: *sonans*. Bruno uses "sounding thing" to mean a vowel.</note>; the second in which a vowel precedes a consonant; and the third in which a vowel is placed between two or three consonants, designated by five different positions. In that riddle—which involves <margin>545</margin> an art opening the way to countless industrious applications—we suggested <margin>10</margin> that a beast be placed in the center of a circle or a square to act as a manifold consonant; it then adopts a manifold vowel for itself according to five different positions. <note>In Bruno’s system, a central image (the beast) represents a base consonant, and its orientation toward different points of the compass or parts of the square indicates which vowel is attached to it (A, E, I, O, or U).</note>

> It roars one way if it looks toward the glowing sunrise,
> Where the horses of the sun first show their brow.
> <margin>15</margin> It does not cry the same when the last steeds of your team,
> O Apollo <note>original: *Phoebe*. A title for the sun god.</note>, turn their gaze toward the evening.
> It sounds different when looking at the watchful Boötes <note>The constellation of the Herdsman, indicating the North.</note>
> Standing over the Nolan soil <note>Bruno refers to his birthplace, Nola, in Italy.</note> by night and day.
> And it sounds not the same when the earth, with its dense body, 
> <margin>20</margin> Turning away, hides the light of the Bear <note>The Great Bear constellation, another northern marker.</note> from you.
> It thunders a fifth sound, different from those mentioned, 
> When the whole beast sits within itself, not unmindful of its own.
> But if a rocky cave catches its voice,
> Where the air is bent back to restore the sound,
> <margin>25</margin> Either an echo resounds for you, or if practiced use strives for it,
> The reversed elements will return a reversed mark. <note>This refers to the ability to read the memory system both forward and backward, or the use of "echo" as a secondary mnemonic layer.</note>

<margin>10</margin>### Explanation of the Interpreter, which is the thirtieth seal.

All the Universal Seals <note>original: "Sigilli universi." These are the core symbolic structures in Bruno's system.</note> that refer to the arrangement of speech, and all the formative methods of vocabularies, can be the subject of this supervening seal. Indeed, <margin>c 3v</margin> unless a word exists beforehand as a subject for interpretation, <margin>15</margin> how could we possibly establish an interpreter by any method? For a person <margin>546</margin> characterized by their homeland, their own place, their art, the work of that art, and the tool through which they represent their formation, let it be understood that whatever is to be signified happens there, where both the agent works conveniently and the operation is more properly <margin>20</margin> carried out. The other matters contained in the thirtieth seal need no explanation; let us only provide this: that we add below three tables as a paradigm for figuring and retaining a Hebrew dictionary <note>Bruno suggests using his mnemonic system to master the Hebrew language, likely by associating letters with these specific images.</note> with the greatest ease.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for Giordano Bruno's mnemonic system, moving from the list of symbolic figures (like the Arithmancer or High Priest) to the spatial organization of these images within "Courts" (atria) and "Tables" (tabulae). It explains how to distribute 22 parts or seats within each mnemonic space.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

<margin>547</margin> The same reasoning applies to the rest. Each of the **Courts** will have twenty-two parts at most, each of which will have seats distributed in the same order, provided the first seat is maintained from which the name of the Court is taken. For example, in the **Court of the River** (which is designated by the letter **L**), the first seat is the **river**, the second is the **fountain**, the third is the **portico**, and the fourth is the **pyramid**; in the **Court of the Furnace**, the first seat is the **furnace**, the second is the **fountain**, the third is the **portico**, and the fourth is the **pyramid**. It is the same in the others. <note>Bruno is describing a "Method of Loci" where the user visualizes a building (a Court) with specific architectural features (seats) to store information. The consistency of the "fountain, portico, pyramid" across different courts helps the practitioner navigate the mental space.</note>

There, the mage, the <term>pyromancer</term><note>original: "pyromantus." A diviner who reads signs in fire.</note>, the <term>geomancer</term><note>original: "geomantus." A diviner who reads patterns in the earth or soil.</note>, and those who follow, can designate either the men, or the courts, or the chambers of the courts.

A square figure is adapted for this Table, consisting of twenty-two rows, each of which has just as many chambers. You should lay out twenty-two tables for yourself after its likeness; at the head of these, you should place the mark of one element, which signifies the **president**; <margin>c 4v</margin> in the chambers of each individual row, you should successively write the mark of another element along the diagonal from the upper right corner to the lower left, which is established to designate the row; in the individual chambers of the rows, you have that third element, which is seen directly above or below, or in the seat itself, so that from there a convenient access may be made: either from the president through each of the twenty-two courts to the twenty-two houses, or from each of the courts through the twenty-two houses of each into the field or to the president. <note>Bruno is describing a complex combinatorial grid, similar to a Vigenère square or the "Great Table" of Ramon Llull, where different sets of symbols (elements, presidents, and houses) intersect to create thousands of unique memory associations.</note>

->On the explanation of the multiple deduction of non-sensible forms from those that are sensible.<-

<margin>10</margin>In how many ways, and by what specific means, non-sensible forms <note>Non-sensible forms are abstract ideas or concepts that cannot be perceived directly by the five senses.</note> are to be figured, noted, and retained through those things which are open to the senses, we have expressed more fully not only here, but also in other places. We have treated this most copiously in one of the volumes of the *Great Key* <note>original: "Clavis magnae."</note>, which is titled the *Seal of Seals*
<margin>15</margin><note>original: "Sigillorum sigillus."</note>. There we are taught how to elicit not only non-sensible forms from sensible ones, but any forms from any others, for all operations of the mind—drawing from natural, artificial, and perhaps even divine principles. For many weighty reasons, we continue that same investigation in the present discussion.

# THE WORKS OF PHILOTHEUS GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA

## THE SEAL OF SEALS

### ADAPTED FOR ACQUIRING ALL DISPOSITIONS OF THE MIND AND PERFECTING ITS HABITS.

---

<margin>5</margin> 1. These things, among others, that divine spirit—which never rests in base <note>original: "sordidis," implying minds that are unrefined or morally cluttered.</note> minds—instilled in me: while you were hesitating and becoming deeply inflamed toward the matter itself, you must first strive for this: that you worship the first and nearest God <note>Bruno often identifies this "nearest God" with the internal light of reason or the world-soul acting within the individual.</note> by whom you are awakened from without and incited from within, that you magnify the prince, invoke the divine power, and behold the light.

2. Remember that there ought to be three stages in every human art: first, each thing should be wisely thought out <term>excogitentur</term> <note>The conceptual stage of planning and internal visualization.</note> before it is made; second, it should be carried out with maturity and vigor; third, those things which have been thought out and brought forth should be preserved and manfully defended.

3. For this reason, antiquity teaches that three Gods preside over all arts: Pallas <note>The goddess of wisdom, representing the intellect and the plan.</note>, Vulcan <note>The god of fire and the forge, representing the active labor of making.</note>, and Mars <note>The god of war, representing the strength required to protect one's discoveries or creations.</note>. This is a certain creative <term>trinity</term> of deities, always standing by Jupiter, the supreme architect of all things, so that <column-break/> <margin>c 7v</margin> just as the whole trinity relates to Jupiter, so Vulcan and Mars relate to Pallas <note>In Bruno’s system, action (Vulcan) and defense (Mars) must always be subordinate to and guided by Wisdom (Pallas).</note>.

<sig>c 8<sup>r</sup></sig>

4. Of these three who reign in the divine art, we see three traces in nature as well: the trace of Pallas is the order by which things are arranged; the trace of Vulcan is swift progress and a readiness, as if hurrying toward birth; and the trace of Mars is the <margin>5</margin> structure passed from those who generate to those who are generated.

5. In this way, individual things also: 1. flow forth from the perennial source; 2. are born; 3. and while they seek their origin again, they flow back into the same: 1. they come to be, 2. they grow to maturity, 3. they are perfected; hence Orpheus called the same thing the **554** <note>This likely refers to a specific citation or page number in the Orphic hymns available to Bruno.</note> beginning, middle, and end.

<margin>10</margin> 6. Indeed, necessity compels you to call forth and attempt this. Placed in a moment of crisis through necessity, man seeks and grasps for the "wings of the dawn" (as they say), by the will of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. He, lest human wit should grow sluggish and its vivid <unclear>force</unclear> <note>original: "vividaque illius emoriatur * * *"; the Latin text has a gap here, likely intended to be "vis" (force/power).</note> die out, added pressing <margin>15</margin> poverty to difficult circumstances.

7. Remember that Prometheus did not please the Gods, insofar as he, by scattering the treasures of the Gods, seemed to incite the human race toward sluggishness, or because he made a most excellent thing common to the worthy and unworthy alike.

<margin>20</margin> 8. May you, therefore, possess within yourself and with a few others a taste of that healing, nectar-like liquor. Once you have thoroughly purged the lethargic humors of the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> with it, you may easily pursue first a celestial life with the celestial Gods, and soon a <term>supracelestial</term> <note>Referring to the realm beyond the physical stars, often associated with pure intellect or the divine presence.</note> circuit with the supracelestial beings. From there, you will look down upon <margin>25</margin> Carneades, Cineas, and Metrodorus <note>Philosophers representing various schools of skepticism or Epicureanism whom Bruno views as intellectually limited.</note> standing no higher than the prostrate multitude of the astonished common people.

10. Nature has granted exquisite wings to all, according to their capacity, but there are very few indeed who know how to unfold them to divide and beat that air. This air must be beaten to assist flight no less than it seems to hinder it by needing to be divided; for after you have moved the air by the labor of dividing it, the air itself, not ungrateful, will push you forward by supporting you. <note>Bruno uses the metaphor of flight to describe intellectual effort: the very "resistance" of difficult study eventually provides the lift needed for higher understanding.</note>

11. Objects, signs, images, specters, or <term>phantasms</term> <note>from the Greek *phantasmata*; in Bruno's philosophy, these are the mental images or "shadows" through which the human mind understands higher truths</note> are presented to us. Their differences consist of the repulsive (which is deformed and evil) and the desirable (which is <margin>555</margin> beautiful and good), and those composed of two or three of these, such as the lovable-good or the repulsive-deformed. Likewise, there is that which is easy to grasp—which is a sensory perception neither excessive nor lacking, combined with an abstract intellectual concept—and that which is difficult to grasp, which is a sensory perception that is either faint or overwhelming, and by its very nature (since it lacks abstraction) highly intelligible.

From this emerges seeing, touching in a general sense, imagining, thinking, the primary act of remembering, reasoning, and understanding. From these arises the "secondary memory," which is usually called the **attained intellect** <note>original: *intellectus adeptus*; a term from medieval Aristotelianism referring to the human intellect when it has been fully actualized by divine or universal truth</note> or the intellect "in habit."
