<summary>This page lists the nine primary Lullian questions (Rules B through K) and explains how to expand a logical investigation by applying these questions to one another and to their sub-categories. This systematic "multiplication" ensures that every possible aspect of a subject—from its essence and quantity to its purpose and location—is thoroughly examined.</summary>

## CONCERNING THOSE THINGS WHICH PERTAIN PRECISELY TO THE SECOND OPERATION OF THE INTELLECT, AND THE THIRD FIGURE OF RAYMOND LULL. Chapter I.
<note>In the logic of this period, the "second operation of the intellect" refers to the mind's ability to form judgments or propositions—joining a subject and a predicate—rather than just understanding a single concept.</note>

### First Part.
<note>original: *I. Membrum*; literally a "limb" or "member," used here as a structural heading.</note>

5 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Although you are able to understand all things for yourself from what has been said above (for in those sections we hold whatever pertains to all operations of the intellect, not merely implicitly, but even most fully explained), nevertheless, this must be noted separately: <margin>g 2<sup>v</sup></margin>
10 just as all things were considered individually (namely, when rules after rules, subjects after subjects, and predicates after predicates were defined to form their simple apprehension <note>original: *simplicem apprehensionem*; the "first operation" of the mind, where one understands a concept without yet making a judgment about it</note>), let them now be considered as they are combined with one another, first for the purpose of constructing propositions,
15 so that the second operation of the intellect may be exercised—namely, composition and division, or affirmation and negation. 20 other signifies the predicate).

This very composition or combination proceeds in a threefold way <note>The text says "threefold" (*tripliciter*), though the author immediately lists four distinct methods. Later editors noted this discrepancy.</note>:

KH, KG, up to eight following terms; HG, HF, HE, up
<margin>10</margin>to six following terms; FE, FD, up to four; ED, EC,
EB, up to three; DC, DB, two; and CB, one.

CD, DE, EF, FG, GH, HI, IK; this chaining is simple,

wherever one begins, by the power of the proposition, all the rings of the

if you begin from chamber HI, saying for example: "true virtue,"

you proceed from there to IK, then KB, BC, CD, and so on. Thus, wher-
<margin>20</margin>ever you begin, you will always be able to run through all the
dwellings, just as if the chambers were arranged in a circle; for
the progression always returns to the point where the beginning was made.

Or it occurs, fourthly, through doubling, as when it is said BB,
CC, DD, EE, FF, GG, HH, II, KK; you will be able to observe
<margin>25</margin>these four orders very easily in the following table.

### Section III.

These are the thirty-six **chambers** <term>camerae | the individual cells or squares in a logical grid where two concepts are combined</term>, which, derived from the triple meaning of the **elements** <note>The letters B through K used in this system to represent fundamental categories such as Goodness, Power, or Wisdom.</note> themselves, establish—in their **evacuation** <term>evacuatione | the systematic process of exhausting all possible logical combinations within the grid</term>—first, twelve propositions;
<margin>5</margin> second, twenty-four questions, which double those twelve propositions by using two rules signified within two elements; third, those which are multiplied by the evacuation of the aforementioned types of rules; fourth, those which are multiplied into twelve intermediate propositions by the interposition of two **means** <note>original: *media*. In logic, the "middle term" that connects the subject and predicate in a syllogism.</note>, also signified by two elements.
<margin>10</margin> This is explained in the sixth part of **Llull's** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the philosopher who invented this combinatorial system of logic.</note> work, both in his **Great Art** <note>original: *Arte magna*</note> and his **Small Art** <note>original: *Arte parva*</note>, in the section "On the Evacuation of the Third Figure." However, these matters are handled more orderly and briefly in **our own writings** <note>original: *in nostris*. Bruno is referring to his own improved versions of Lullian mnemonic and logical systems.</note>, where it is sufficient to have provided an example in **chamber BC** <note>The specific grid cell where the concepts represented by B and C intersect.</note>, 
<margin>15</margin> as all other chambers follow the same pattern. All these things can be perfectly understood and judged through the points we have noted here.

## ON THE THINGS PERTAINING TO THE FOURTH FIGURE AND THE THIRD OPERATION OF THE INTELLECT. | CHAPTER III.

->Part I.<-

<margin>5</margin>It follows now to consider those things pertaining to the **fourth figure** <note>A combinatorial device consisting of three concentric circles used to find the "middle term" of a logical argument.</note> proposed by **Llull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the philosopher whose mnemonic and logical system Bruno is expanding upon.</note>, from which is forged the **third operation of the intellect** <term>tertia intellectus operatio | in classical logic, this is the process of reasoning or "argumentation," where the mind moves from known premises to a new conclusion.</term>, which is argumentation.

The fourth figure is therefore composed of three circles, <margin>10</margin>of which the uppermost <note>original: *superior*. Referring to the outermost circle of the diagram.</note> is always immobile, while the two lower <note>The inner circles.</note> are mobile, as is evident in the present diagram.

<margin>g 5^v</margin> Where both ends <note>The outermost and innermost circles.</note> remain immobile, and the **B** of the middle circle is positioned beneath the **B** of the upper circle and above the **B** of the lowest circle, nine **chambers** <term>camerae | in Lullian logic, a "chamber" is a specific cell or grouping of terms in a combinatorial table.</term> are produced, which consist of the nine elements tripled <note>e.g., BBB, CCC, etc.</note>. Then, when the **C** of the middle circle is placed beneath the **B** of the upper circle and above the **B** of the lower circle, nine other chambers are produced, <margin>5</margin> namely: **BCB, CDC, DED, EFE, FGF, GHG, HIH, IKI, KBK**. Next, by moving the **D** of the middle circle between the two **Bs** of the upper and lower circles, nine other chambers are produced: **BDB, CEC, DFD, EGE, FHF, GIG, HKH, IBI, KCK**. <margin>10</margin> Similarly, by moving all the other seven elements beneath the **B** of the upper circle and the **B** of the lower circle, just as many sets of nine chambers are acquired. Thus, just as the process was carried out by moving the middle circle beneath the two [fixed] circles, it can proceed similarly in the multiplication of these chambers by moving the lowest circle beneath the two upper ones.

You have, therefore, the designated **columns** and **chambers**: the columns are those which consist of several chambers and represent the **total variation** itself, which is created by one movement of one element <margin>20</margin><margin>694</margin> beneath or between others. The chambers, however, are the parts of the | columns themselves, which in this proposal all consist of **three elements**. From this, the logic for constructing the table according to its proper order becomes clear.

...great [table], which is formed by the **T** itself being added and arranged in various ways.

<margin>5</margin> The **T** itself is positioned to signify a variation of the terms, so that you may know when the elements <note>The letters B through K used in Llull's system.</note> signify terms of the **First Figure** <note>The "First Figure" represents absolute attributes of being, such as Goodness, Greatness, and Power.</note>, and when they signify terms of the **Second Figure** <note>The "Second Figure" represents relative concepts used to compare the absolute attributes, such as Difference, Agreement, or Contrariety.</note>. For the letters placed before the **T** always signify terms of the First Figure, and letters after the **T** signify terms of the Second Figure. Thus, when **T** is placed at the beginning, all the terms belong to the First Figure.

Here, where **BCTB** is written, it signifies **great goodness differing** <note>original: "bonitas magna differens"</note> or goodness having a great difference;
<margin>10</margin> **BTCB** signifies **goodness differing through concordance** <note>original: "bonitas differens per concordantiam"</note> (for things are not said to "concord" or agree unless they differ by some means, and all things said to agree must differ in some way; for a thing is not said to agree with itself);
<margin>15</margin> **TBCB** signifies the **difference of the agreeing and the differing**, or the difference between that which agrees and that which differs;
**BCBT** i.e., **great goodness capable of being made good** <note>original: "bonitas magna bonificabilis"</note>, or of the one making good, or of the thing made good, or to make good with great goodness.

Behold how from one "chamber" <term>camera | a specific grouping of three or four letters in the Lullian combinatorial system.</term> of the preceding
<margin>20</margin> table, another column arises through the various
<margin>g 6^v</margin> arrangements of the **T** itself, as is evident | in the first column of Llull, which is indeed formed from the chamber **BCD**, sometimes with **B** preceding, sometimes with **C** preceding, sometimes with **D** preceding, and with the **T** itself situated among those three elements in various ways according to the
<margin>25</margin> aforementioned method.

<margin>g 7ʳ</margin>
## ON THE USE OF THE THIRD AND FOURTH FIGURES
## AND THE GENERAL TABLE.

Since the operation of the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus operatio"; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the three stages of reasoning: forming concepts, making judgments, and drawing conclusions.</note> is threefold, as we have shown in the preceding sections, it happens that we employ a combination of terms in all of them: in the first by **defining**, in the second by **verifying**, and in the third by **arguing**. We **define** when we say "a mortal rational animal," which are terms represented by the letters **EG** <note>In the Lullian system, letters like E and G represent specific categories or principles on the logical wheels.</note>. We **verify** <note>original: "verificando"; meaning to state a true proposition or judgment.</note> when we say "man is a mortal rational animal," which terms are also represented by **FG**. We **argue** <note>original: "argumentamur"; the act of constructing a syllogism to prove a point.</note> when we say: "every being that uses reason, or is capable of reasoning, is a rational animal; man is a certain being capable of reasoning; therefore, man is a rational animal." These terms <margin>696</margin> are represented | by **EFG**, where **F** signifies the <term>middle term</term> <note>original: "medium"; the crucial third term in a syllogism that connects the subject and the predicate.</note>, by means of which the predicate itself (the definition) is joined to the subject (the thing being defined).

Therefore, through the **Third Figure**, we obtain both definitions and propositions, both of which consist of two terms; for a definition is forged from a <term>genus</term> and a <term>difference</term> <note>A "genus" is a general category (like "animal"), and a "difference" is the specific trait that distinguishes a species within that category (like "rational").</note>, while a proposition is made from a <term>subject</term> and a <term>predicate</term>.

<margin>g 7ᵛ</margin>
Furthermore, through the **Fourth Figure**, it is possible to **define** when we take a genus along with several | differences, as when we say "a mortal rational animal." It is also possible to **verify** with three or more terms, as when we say "God is great in power and wisdom." It is also possible to **demonstrate** when we take various terms between the subject and the predicate—for instance, between one term represented by the upper circle of the Third Figure and the lower circle of the same.

He demonstrates how combinations of symbolic letters (E, F, G) represent the relationship between subjects, predicates, and middle terms.</summary>

...middle [terms] to demonstrate that the meaning signified by the element of the lowest circle is predicated of the meaning signified by the element of the upper circle, in such a way that the middle circle always signifies the cause or the "medium" <note>In logic, the "middle term" (medium) is the bridge that connects the subject and the predicate in a syllogism.</note> on account of which the predicate is said of the subject. 

Let this be shown by the following example. Suppose you wish to demonstrate that God is omnipotent. You have "God" as your subject and "omnipotent" as your predicate. Therefore, arrange the element **B** in the upper circle to signify the subject, which is God, and **E** in the lowest circle to signify the predicate, which is "supreme power" <note>In Bruno’s system, based on Ramon Llull, the letter B usually represents Goodness or the first member of a set, and E represents Power.</note>. To demonstrate and prove this, it is necessary to investigate and find a middle term or cause. Therefore, while keeping the uppermost and lowermost circles stationary, let the other elements be brought between those two in order by rotating the middle circle. 

First, place **B** between the two aforementioned letters and state the combination **BBE**, that is: "everything that is self-diffusing <note>original: "diffusivum sui ipsius"; a common philosophical principle stating that "the good is self-diffusive," meaning it naturally shares or pours itself out.</note> (which is one of the characteristics of Goodness) possesses the power by which it diffuses itself; God is supremely self-diffusing; therefore, He is <margin>g 8r</margin> supremely | powerful or omnipotent." 

Or it may be done thus: "everything that is supremely goodness-making can, in the highest degree, do good, and consequently has power in the highest degree; <margin>697</margin> God | is supremely goodness-making and consequently, etc., therefore, etc." 

Next, in the place of that middle **B**, let **C** succeed it, stating the combination **BCE**: "everything that knows all things, or is supremely knowing, has power over all things or possesses supreme power; God is supreme and understands above all things; therefore, He possesses supreme power, or is omnipotent." 

The same can be done through other middle terms. Indeed, these middle terms are not only the terms explicitly stated in this Art, but there can also be countless others, as we taught above, by arranging "houses" <note>In mnemonics and Lullism, "houses" (domos) are mental or visual locations where specific concepts are stored for retrieval.</note> for the terms—

Thus, the more terms you provide for yourself—by expanding and filling the "houses" <note>original: "domos"; another term for the logical categories in his system.</note> we have ordered to be established—the more and more certain middle terms <note>In logic, the "middle term" is the bridge that connects the subject and the predicate in a syllogism.</note> you will have. By these, you will be able to demonstrate the same conclusion, not from futile and empty multiplicity, but from proper and necessary reasons. Whether Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the Majorcan philosopher who invented the system of rotating wheels that Bruno expanded upon.</note> reached this point, consider for yourself; and weigh how much has been added to this art by us.

Once you have run through the revolution of the middle circle by forming the chamber **BE**—which adopts a middle term from all nine elements of a single figure (such as the first figure)—with the letter **T** <note>In this system, "T" often acts as a relational operator, helping to link terms together.</note> following, saying it in the form **BBET**, **BCET**, **BDET**, and so on, you will then be able to arrange new arguments. <margin>5</margin>From what has been said above, it is established that it is very easy for us to adopt <note>original: "adsciscere"</note> innumerable <term>middle terms</term> <note>In a logical syllogism, the "middle term" is the concept that connects the subject and the predicate to reach a conclusion. <margin>18</margin>to strike out the light and fire hiding beneath, as if from a dense and black flintstone. Among these, I was able to see one who was otherwise of a not entirely common talent and judgment, who in
<margin>20</margin>a certain book entitled *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "De vanitate scientiarum"; this refers to the famous work by Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, published in 1526, which attacked all forms of human knowledge, including the Lullian art Bruno champions here.</note> (where the title itself, unless perhaps that ironic conclusion of the same book deceives me, expressed more than enough what kind of pursuit is in the work’s progress), says that this art
<margin>25</margin>consists in abundance, order, ostentation, and as if in a certain broadening of the fringes <note>original: "fimbriarum dilatatione"; a biblical allusion (Matthew 23:5) suggesting the art is merely a showy, superficial display of piety or knowledge without substance.</note>, so that it produces not knowledge and some ma- <note>The text cuts off here at "ma-", likely intending "materiâ" (matter) or "maiestatem" (majesty).</note>

...making contemplation significant, and how much of a reputation for many-sided learning and deeper knowledge it produces. Furthermore, <margin>**699**</margin> that man <note>Bruno is referring to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, who famously criticized the "vanity" of all sciences, including the Lullian Art Bruno champions.</note> says nothing about this art that could not also be said of all other faculties and sciences (except for that one which he himself seems to extol at the end). For in all things, no one—unless they are more than moderately foolish—will believe they have attained a true knowledge, untainted by vanity, after all their study. Indeed, even he who seems to have attributed the most to human genius among all philosophers, Aristotle, testifies to this where he says that the substances of things and their ultimate differences are unnamable and imperceptible, and that the eye of our intelligence relates to the most manifest things of nature in no other way than the eyes of a nocturnal bird <note>original: "nocturnae avis"; This is the "Owl of Aristotle" metaphor from the *Metaphysics*. Just as an owl is blinded by the bright sun, human reason is overwhelmed by the most fundamental truths of nature.</note> relate to the light of the sun. I pass over those who, defining truth as residing in the thickest darkness, thought they had known the most and reached the summit of philosophy when they realized they were not ignorant of their own ignorance <note>A reference to Socratic irony—the idea that the only true wisdom is knowing that you know nothing.</note>. Therefore, what is finally possible to obtain through all the sciences is acquired through this art, as if through a most general cause. But if the other sciences offer nothing of great importance beyond a mere reputation, it is enough that this art contains something beyond reputation—something which that man either did not penetrate at all, or not sufficiently.

## II. Section. <note>original: "Membrum"; literally "a limb," used here to denote a major division of the chapter.</note>

Regarding our purpose, then, it must be noted that since there exists a manifold kind of argumentation and artificial demonstration—for instance, from those things which are more ready <note>original: "promptiora"; referring to things that are obvious or easily accessible to our senses</note> to our hand, from those which are better known according to nature, and from those which are better known and prior according to being and according to cog- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "cognitionem" (knowledge).</note>

<meta>This page continues Bruno's technical discussion of logical demonstration, moving from the Aristotelian limits of knowledge mentioned on the previous page to a specific classification of how we prove truths. He bridges the gap between traditional "Peripatetic" (Aristotelian) logic and the specific "Art" of Ramon Llull.</meta>

<page-num>325</page-num>
<header>ON THE COMBINATORIAL LAMP. 325</header>

...knowledge <note>The text begins mid-word, "gnitionem," continuing from the previous page's "recognitionem."</note> in the same way, just as it is sufficiently well-known that there is a certain order in mathematics. A triple type of demonstration is introduced, not without reason, by certain Arabic Peripatetics <term>Peripatetic Arabibus: Arabic-speaking followers of Aristotle's philosophy, such as Avicenna or Averroes, who refined Greek logic</term>: namely, *demonstration simply* (or of the cause in general); 
<margin>5</margin> *demonstration of the "wherefore"* (or of the cause of being); and *demonstration of the "that"* (or of the cause of knowing, also called the "sign"). | They define *demonstration simply* <margin>700</margin> as that which comes from prior causes and principles, from which the thing itself is both made and first known—just as the point, the line, and the angle relate to geometric figures. They call the *demonstration of the sign* <margin>10</margin> that which proceeds from prior elements | of the kind through which a thing only begins to be known for the first time. <margin>h 2v</margin> Truly, the *demonstration of the "wherefore"* <note>original: "propter quid"</note> is that which runs from the causes of being—which are further removed from sense and reason—to the effect itself. We approve of this division as being more than sufficient in its kind, even though the Greek <margin>15</margin> commentators did not touch upon it, and Aristotle did not express it as clearly as would be enough for ignorant or duller minds.

### Part III.

To this triple type of demonstration—which seems to be composed of two modes of priority and one of posteriority—
<margin>20</margin> we add a fourth mode, which you might call "from equals" or "co-evals." This mode is drawn from those things which neither precede nor follow the subject, but are carried along with it; when the subject is established, these are necessarily established and define it. 
<margin>25</margin> This specific type of demonstration is peculiar to Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the Majorcan philosopher whose "Art" of combining concepts Bruno championed.</note>, and it is the most certain kind that can be used for confirming a predicate regarding any subject. He explained this through his suffixes: *-ive*, *-able*, and *-ing* <note>original: "ivum, abile et are"; These are the three components of a Lullian "Dignity" or principle. For example, in the principle of Goodness, there is that which makes things good (Bonificative), that which can be made good (Bonificable), and the act of making good (Bonifying).</note>.

<summary>Bruno outlines three traditional Aristotelian methods of logical proof (demonstration) before introducing a fourth, superior method derived from Ramon Llull. This "Lullian" method relies on the intrinsic, simultaneous relationship between the power, the capacity, and the action of a thing.</summary>

<keywords>logic, demonstration, Aristotle, Ramon Llull, Arabic Peripatetics, causes of being, Lullian suffixes, epistemology</keywords>

--- Page 338 ---
<meta>This page continues Bruno's analysis of logical demonstration. While the previous page categorized demonstrations based on causes (the "wherefore") and signs (the "that"), Bruno now introduces a "truer" method derived from the intrinsic nature of things, utilizing the technical suffixes of the Lullian Art to explain how a thing's essence is revealed through its internal activity rather than just its external effects.</meta>

<page-num>326</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>OF GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

From here, one may take up the most certain and truest method of demonstration. For from what source can we better argue that something is good than from the fact that it is "good-ive" <note>original: *ivum*. This is a technical suffix used by Bruno and Ramon Llull to denote the internal power or capacity for action within an essence.</note>, which is to say, that it possesses an intrinsic principle of doing good or acting well? Or than from the fact that it possesses "to-be-ing" <note>original: *are*. This represents the infinitive or the actual exercise of a power.</note>, 
<margin>h 3r</margin> that is, the act of doing good, because it acts well | or effects good? This is like arguing that the sun is hot because it heats, or bright because it shines; or that the moon is luminous from the fact that it is illuminated, which is through "ed-ness" <note>original: *atum*. This represents the passive or resultant state of an action.</note>. This is not a matter of showing a truth through an effect, 
<margin>701</margin> nor | through a cause, nor through both. For when I show the truth of the sun through its own light, I do not show it through an effect; for light is not an "effect" of the sun, any more than heat is an effect of fire—since heat is its very form, a subject constantly accompanying it. Rather, it is that light which is diffused from the sun into a body capable of being illuminated, and that heat which is impressed upon a subject capable of being heated, which are the true "effects" of the sun and fire. 

Therefore, such "to-be-ing" and "ed-ness" <note>original: *are et atum*</note>—that is, such an acting and such a being affected by nature—insinuate the truth of a thing not from an external effect nor from a prior cause, but from that which is within the thing itself. Likewise, in those things which are coordinated and inseparable from one another (as is also manifest in the existence of correlatives <term>Correlatives: terms that define each other, like "parent" and "child," where one cannot exist without the other</term> and contraries), it is possible to demonstrate most powerfully apart from the reasoning of cause and effect. But it must suffice for the present to have indicated the place of this consideration, since we have spoken about this very thing more extensively elsewhere <note>Bruno likely refers to his work *De la causa, principio et uno* (On Cause, Principle, and Unity), published in 1584.</note>. 

As for the manner in which it is permitted to state something about a subject based on things appropriated to and fitting that subject—such as the parts and principles that remain permanent in the finished deed, as well as its proper attributes—we have sufficiently demonstrated this in the preceding sections.

<summary>Bruno argues for a method of demonstration based on a thing's internal essence and activity (using Lullian terms like ivum, are, and atum) rather than external causes or effects. He distinguishes between intrinsic properties, like the sun's light, and their external impacts on other objects.</summary>

### IV. Part.

<margin>h 3<sup>v</sup></margin>
<margin>702</margin>
Therefore, we have so completed this art, which was originally devised by Ramon Llull <note>original: *Raymundo Lullio*. Llull was a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher who created a logical system of rotating wheels to discover universal truths.</note>, and have so vindicated it from every pretext of scorn, that it may be recognized to have so fully filled its own proper sphere that it is entirely impossible to add anything further to it (regarding its like elements). If, however, there are matters that seem to require a broader explanation—such as the larger and expanded model of the Great Table <note>The "Great Table" is a complex diagram in the Lullian system used to calculate all possible combinations of basic concepts.</note>—all these and other things pertaining to their circumstances have been most sufficiently explained in detail by us in the book *On the Architecture of the Lullian Art* <note>original: *De architectura artis Lullianae*. This refers to another of Bruno's works where he expands on the mechanical and structural aspects of Llull's logic.</note>. The specific aims of that treatment, when added to these present ones, will make it clear that we have overlooked nothing that belongs to the capability and use of the present art. Whoever you are, therefore, who will be a reader and student of these things, if until now you have been less successful in grasping these aims, pray to God that through repeated efforts you may achieve them; for the more deeply you ponder them with your intellect, the more inward will be the praises you bring forth for this discovery, and the greater the thanks you will give to Llull as the inventor, to me as the refiner <note>original: *excultori*. Bruno views himself as the one who "cultivated" or polished Llull's raw insights into a finished science.</note>, and to God as the giver of all good things.

TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND EXCELLENT LORD

# DON GUILLERMO DE SAN CLEMENTE

->KNIGHT OF THE ORDER OF SAINT JAMES OF THE SWORD,<-
->COUNSELOR TO THE MOST SERENE CATHOLIC KING OF THE SPAINS AND HIS<-
->AMBASSADOR TO THE IMPERIAL MAJESTY OF EMPEROR RUDOLF II<-

### GIORDANO BRUNO THE NOLAN SENDS GREETINGS.

Just as no one considers mute animals to be of noble stock—even if born from highly praised parents—unless those animals are also strong, so too men cannot be rightly called "noble" unless they have distinguished <margin>10</margin> themselves by their own personal virtue. For this reason, among the three <note>Though the text says "three," Bruno proceeds to list four distinct types, a common rhetorical structure in his era.</note> types of nobility enumerated by Plato: the first <margin>a 2v</margin> | is that which is derived from wise, upright, and just ancestors; the second, that which comes from heroes and princes; the third, that which is passed down to posterity from those who have either conducted the business of war with distinction or have carried <margin>15</margin> away the crowns of victory in great contests. Finally, a fourth type is judged by that same philosopher to be the most excellent of all: that by which a man, through the greatness of his own soul, surpasses the common crowd. For if a man is disposed otherwise, and is compared at any time to his own great ancestors, then that line of Persius <note>original: "Persianum"; while Bruno attributes this to the satirist Persius, these verses are actually from Juvenal’s Satires (8, 51–53).</note> will not <margin>20</margin> unjustly be drummed into his ears:

> This industrious youth seeks the Euphrates and the
> eagle-standards guarding the conquered Batavians <note>The "Batavians" were a Germanic tribe; the "eagles" refer to the standards of the Roman legions.</note> in arms; but as for you,
> you are nothing but a descendant of Cecrops <note>A "Cecropides" or descendant of Cecrops (the mythical founder of Athens) implies someone boasting of ancient, royal lineage.</note>, most like a marble bust of Hermes. <note>original: "truncoque simillimus Hermae"; a "Herm" was a squared stone pillar topped with a head, lacking the limbs necessary for action.</note>

<summary>In this dedication, Giordano Bruno argues that true nobility is defined by individual virtue and "greatness of soul" rather than mere inheritance or ancient lineage. He addresses the Spanish ambassador to the Imperial court, setting a philosophical tone that values personal merit over status.</summary>

->His head is of marble; your image is alive —<-
<note>original: "Nullo quippe alio vincis discrimine, quam quod / Illi marmoreum caput est, tua vivit imago." This concludes a quotation from Juvenal’s Satires (8.54–55), which Bruno previously misattributed to Persius. It contrasts a living, virtuous man with the lifeless statues of his ancestors.</note>

<margin>604</margin> Most noble and truly magnanimous Lord, you have most excellently guarded against this: that you—being renowned not solely by the hereditary splendor of your ancestors—might shine forth for so many reasons and in so many ways <margin>a 3r</margin> | with every kind of distinction arising from yourself and acquired by your own efforts. I shall refrain from enumerating these reasons, both because they are manifest, and because they are greater than can or should be treated in a summary and oratorical style suited to this place.

These very reasons are why, when I was seeking a patron for this Lullian invention <note>Referring to the "Great Art" of Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a system of logic and combinatorics that Bruno spent much of his career expanding.</note> and for my own studies regarding it—a patron who would be powerful in both judgment and authority—your most illustrious Excellence seemed, above all others, the most desirable. I chose to entrust the study of this sublime art to your patronage so that I might not be seen, perhaps, to tell a story to the deaf, present a mirror to the blind, or offer the armor of the leader Achilles to Thersites <note>In the *Iliad*, Thersites was a common soldier known for being ugly and cowardly; Bruno uses him as a foil to the hero Achilles to describe someone unworthy of a noble gift.</note>. 

Therefore, this Lullius of yours—who is your fellow countryman <note>Ramon Llull was from Majorca, then part of the Crown of Aragon, as was the ambassador Guillermo de San Clemente.</note>—fleeing toward your heroic spirit and genius, will (I am certainly convinced) be received just as it happened that he himself arrived at your doorstep, as if to his own home, with a more joyful spirit. There, I see it is no less recognized that I have labored to cultivate his invention <margin>a 3v</margin> |—that divinity of understanding which the chief princes of philosophers have been accustomed to admire in the past, and which they must perpetually pursue and imitate in the future. From this source, those whose talents are less known and accessible to the few—in proportion to how much more divine and profound they are—confess to have drawn from the springs of mysteries that lie hidden in the manifold torrent of his teaching.

<summary>Bruno dedicates his work on Lullian logic to the Spanish ambassador, arguing that the ambassador's personal merit makes him the ideal patron for such a profound and "divine" art. He emphasizes that Ramon Llull is a countryman of the ambassador, creating a cultural bond between the patron and the subject matter.</summary>

# ON THE INQUIRY INTO SPECIES.
<note>original: "DE SPECIERVM SCRVTINIO." This refers to the investigation of "species" or logical categories within the system of Ramon Llull.</note>

Having drunk their fill of his abundance, very many people have striven to acquire a name and glory for themselves; through their own commentaries on these matters, they labored not so much to clarify Llull as to illustrate their own names through a strained <note>original: "adtentatum," suggesting a forced or superficial attempt.</note> version of Llull. Now, as to what 
<margin>5</margin> I have finally provided regarding him, let the judgment be yours and that of others who are not deprived of the light of intelligence. 
Under these two titles—*The Lamp* and *The Inquiry*—we certainly embrace those things which can easily suffice for those 
<margin>605</margin> investigating, understanding, and pursuing with judgment all the arts of Llull, <margin>10</margin> provided they have been even moderately versed in the meanings of the terms of common philosophy. For here we seem to have fully 
<margin>a 4r</margin> expressed whatever that most excellent author includes in his many arts, in which he strives to reveal the same invention, now by one 
<margin>15</margin> path (as he himself says), now by another. Indeed, we believe we have condensed into this work a compendium of whatever he suggests in many of his writings for the fulfillment of the divine combinatory art <note>The "combinatory art" refers to Llull’s method of using revolving concentric circles marked with letters representing philosophical categories to generate all possible truths.</note>: in the *Short Art*, the *Great Art*, the *Inventive Art*, the *Demonstrative Art*, the *Mixture of Principles*, the *Cabalistic Hearing*, the 
<margin>20</margin> *Tree of Science*, and many others, if any others exist (as surely many on the same subject must exist). To these I shall add something of great importance, which that divine man concealed and sealed under the aforementioned titles of *The Cabalistic Hearing* and *The Sevenfold Tree*. These 
<margin>25</margin> I shall shortly bring to light (God willing) under the title of *The Cabalistic Lamp*, to be joined to this related art, so that they may stand most safely under that same protection and favor 
<margin>a 4v</margin> of your most illustrious Excellence. | Meanwhile, let [your Excellence] receive from me...

<summary>Bruno criticizes previous scholars for using Ramon Llull's fame for their own gain and asserts that his new works, *The Lamp* and *The Inquiry*, provide a definitive and condensed guide to Llull's complex logical system.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Llull, combinatory art, logic, Cabala, philosophy, book titles, patronage, Giordano Bruno</keywords>

# ON THE INVESTIGATION OF SPECIES.

<margin>Folio 5r, 606</margin>

# ON THE LULLIAN INVESTIGATION OF SPECIES.

---

### Chapter I. The Objective.

To one looking more deeply, it is evident that every art and every discipline—because it either imitates nature, corrects her when she wanders <note>original: *exorbitantem*. Bruno suggests that art can "straighten" nature when it deviates from its ideal form.</note>, or overcomes her when she is resistant—first receives certain principles and elements; secondly, it joins these into simpler combinations; and finally, it draws out more complex and varied structures from those simple ones. From these structures, the specific differences of things certainly arise, which may be compared to numbers of this kind <note>In the Pythagorean and Lullian traditions, "numbers" were often seen as the fundamental ratios or logical structures that define different species of things.</note>.

The skillful understanding of all these matters is finally presented by us, to be viewed at last in its true colors, through this method of investigation which Lull <term>Lullus: refers to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan polymath who created a "Great Art" using combinatory diagrams to find universal truths.</term> first discovered by sketching and outlining it.

The alphabet of this art comprises only nine elements, each of which serves in turn with a fourfold meaning <note>original: *quadruplicis significati*. Bruno is using the Lullian method where a single letter (like B) represents a Subject, an Absolute Predicate, a Relative Predicate, and a Question simultaneously, depending on how it is used in a logical "wheel" or diagram.</note>.

### Chapter III. On the first figure.

The first figure, which is marked by the letter A, encompasses the **absolute predicates**. These are stated—whether affirmed or denied—concerning any subject whatsoever, and can be expressed essentially <note>original: *quidditative*. From the "quiddity" or "what-ness" of a thing; describing its core essence.</note> or by way of an attribute <note>original: *denominative*. Describing a quality assigned to a thing rather than its essence.</note>, in the concrete or in the abstract, interchangeably or non-interchangeably, and in the direct or the oblique case <note>In Latin grammar, the "direct" case is the nominative (the subject), while "oblique" cases are those like the genitive or accusative which show relationship or action.</note>. This is indicated in the figure by lines drawn from the points on the circumference of each element to all the others; this signifies that these elements are predicated not only of everything outside the figure, but also each one is predicated of all the others established within the figure.

### Chapter IV. On the second figure.

The second figure is marked by the letter T, for <margin>608</margin> it is fashioned from the arrangement of three interlaced triangles. To the corners of these triangles, all the **relative terms** are referred as if to their own proper heads <note>In Lullian logic, Figure T represents relations like "Beginning, Middle, End" or "Difference, Concord, Contrariety." These are grouped into three triangles (three groups of three).</note>, and we can indeed contemplate this relationship.

To the right of the grouping, the word "utpote" is also positioned next to "are". ->**-able** as in **capable of being a principle**.<-

->**in -to** as in **to act as a principle**.<-
->**-ed** as in **produced as a principle**.<-
->**-and** as in **needing to be principled**.<-

OF GIORDANO BRUNO
<sig>a 6v</sig>

Which are:
* Form, or the formal principle.
* The subject, or the material principle.
* The efficient [cause], or the agent.
* The action, or the operation.
* The act, or the effect.
* That which is to be done, or the end <note>original: *finis*. In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" or purpose of a thing.</note>.

### Chapter V. On the third figure.

The third figure does not have a unique element of its own to signify. Indeed, in this Art, it expresses the "syllabic" type and the first kind of combination. This is because from the union of two elements, many offspring of **intentions** <note>original: *intentionum*. In logic, an "intention" is a mental concept or the way the mind directs itself toward an object.</note> are propagated. In this figure, one takes either an absolute term with another absolute, an absolute with a relative, a relative with a relative, or a relative with an absolute. These are used either adjectivally or substantively, and thus either on the part of one term or the other. They are taken in either the direct or the oblique case <note>Refers to Latin grammar: the "direct" case is the subject (nominative), while "oblique" cases (genitive, dative, etc.) show relationships like possession or direction.</note>—either both of them or just one—signifying either concretely or abstractly, and this either simply or in a contracted form, through either the first or the second figure.

### Chapter VI. On the fourth figure.

<sig>a 7r</sig>
The fourth figure, formed by three concentric circles, is the most fertile mother of the general table.

### The fourth house, consisting of four rows, has 10 chambers.

The fourth house is formed by the rotation of two circles under the **E** of the stationary circle <note>The "stationary circle" is the outermost ring of Bruno's mnemonic wheel, which does not move.</note>, with the following placements: first, **F** of the middle circle and **G** of the lower circle are placed under it; <margin>5</margin> second, **G** of the middle and **H** of the lowest; third, **H** of the middle and **I** of the lowest; fourth, **I** of the middle and **K** of the lowest.

### The seventh house, consisting of one chamber.

The seventh house is formed by moving **I** of the middle circle and **K** of the lowest circle under the **H** of the stationary circle.

<margin>5</margin> ->1.<-
->hik.<-

->Comparison <note>original: *Comp.* likely for *Comparatio* (comparison) or *Complexio* (combination).</note><-

From the revolution of the circles of the fourth figure, there result twenty-eight houses, of which the first has seven rows and 24 chambers; the second, six rows and 21 chambers; <margin>10</margin> the third, five rows and 15 chambers; the fourth, four rows and 10 chambers; the fifth, three rows and 6 chambers; the sixth, two rows and 3 chambers; the seventh, one chamber.

### Concerning the Great Table. Chapter VII.

The Great Table consists of eighty-four columns, <margin>15</margin> matching the number of chambers described above, which are distributed across 28 rows; these, in turn, are located within the seven houses established by the seven revolutions in the fourth figure.

Each column, moreover, consists of 24 cylinders, and each of these consists of four members. Thus, the number four <margin>20</margin> multiplied by 24 results in 96 members.

The 24 Cylinders are: BCD. CBD. DBC. BDC. CDB. DCB. BBC. BBD. CCB. CCD. DDB. DDC. BCC. BDD. CBB. CDD. DBB. DCC. BCB. BDB. CBC. CDC. DBD. DCD.

# ### CONCERNING THE SCRUTINY OF SPECIES <note>original: *DE SPECIERVM SCRVTINIO* — This refers to the investigation or classification of different types of mental forms or "species" used in the memory system.</note>

<margin>5</margin>Each of the cylinders adopts four members through the fourfold positioning of the letter **T** itself; for **T** is either before the first element (**TBCD**), after the first and before the second (**BTCD**), after the second and before the third (**BCTD**), or after the third (**BCDT**). Elements placed before the **T** signify absolute predicates <note>term: *absolute predicates* — fundamental qualities that exist in themselves, such as "Goodness" or "Greatness."</note>, while elements after the **T** signify relative predicates <note>term: *relative predicates* — qualities that exist in relation to something else, such as "Difference" or "Relation."</note>. **612** The order is established so that **T** is first in the first position, second in the second, third in the third, and fourth in the fourth.

<margin>b 1ᵛ</margin>

|---|---|
| **BCD** | **Column** |
| <margin>10</margin>**tbcd** | difference, concept, containment |
| **btcd** | goodness, concept, containment |
| **bctd** | goodness, magnitude, containment |
| **bcdt** | goodness, magnitude, duration |
| **CBD** | |
| <margin>15</margin>**tcbd** | concept, difference, containment |
| **ctbd** | magnitude, goodness, containment |
| **cbtd** | magnitude, goodness, containment |
| **cbdt** | magnitude, goodness, duration |
| **DBC** | |
| <margin>20</margin>**tdbc** | containment, difference, concept |
| **dtbc** | duration, difference, concept |

### On useful and useless combinations.

Therefore, of the eight sets of twelve <note>original: *duodenariis*, referring to groups of twelve permutations</note> which are contained in the members of this column,
<margin>20</margin> only four are found to be useful. The reason for this is manifest: the sign of the same predicate is doubled in vain in those combinations which are marked in the column by the addition of stars. The first set of twelve is extracted from the first three cylinders <note>The "cylinders" are the concentric rotating wheels of Bruno's memory device</note>; the second from the six following
<margin>25</margin> second wheels; the third from the twelve third and final wheels.
This column of 100 members, of which we have said 48 are <margin>b 3<sup>r</sup></margin> useful, is more fertile <note>original: *foecundior*</note> than the Lullian column, which contains only 20. <note>Bruno is comparing his expanded system to that of Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher who pioneered this combinatorial logic.</note>

<meta>This page continues Bruno's critique and expansion of the Lullian art. On the previous page, he began distinguishing between useful and "useless" (redundant) combinations in the logic wheels. Here, he argues that the order of terms (like BCD vs CBD) creates distinct logical meanings, which Raymond Lull had previously dismissed as mere repetition.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...it consists only of members in a single cylinder. However, it has happened that we enriched it beyond the reasoning by which Raymond <note>Referring to Raymond Lull, the 13th-century philosopher who invented this system of logic</note> might have omitted the other members; for he saw it as a useless repetition of the same thing, since saying **BCD**, that is 
<margin>615</margin>
**great enduring goodness** <note>original: *bonitas magna durans*</note>, and saying **CBD**, that is **enduring great goodness** <note>original: *magna bonitas durans*</note>, is the same thing. We, however, do not disapprove of Raymond's order and sufficiency, and we admit that in his <term>vigenarium</term> <note>a system based on twenty fundamental principles</note> everything is indeed eventually contained, but in a blind way and perhaps even hidden or less considered by Lull himself. 

Therefore, after we have extended the combinations that can be made from these four ordered elements, and it has been revealed which of them all are <term>frugal</term> <note>meaning productive or logically valid</note>, let the column be traversed by taking the first element substantively <note>as a noun or the subject</note> and the two remaining elements adjectivally <note>as descriptors</note>, saying: "great enduring goodness," which is signified in **BCD**. Would not another arrangement of the same elements be most useful and even necessary for the completion of the discourse, by saying: "good enduring magnitude," the sign of which is **CBD**? It is certainly not a repetition of the same thing. 

Similarly, it will never be a repetition of the same thing if the three terms are arranged according to a certain law through the adjective and substantive, the <term>direct and oblique</term> <note>referring to the grammatical cases, where the "direct" is the subject and "oblique" are other cases like the possessive or objective</note>, so that one member behaves according to the same law as another; 
<margin>b 3v</margin>
or if all members are taken in a uniform manner, there will never be a repetition of the same thing, and we do not fall into the omission of something necessary, as happens when **CBD** is neglected once **BCD** has been placed.

->The Number of Laws.<-

Now, the laws by which the column is uniformly traversed are eight, one of which is taking the first term adjectivally—

***

<note>Critical notes: Line 7-8: "in his vigenarium" appears in variant G; line 15: "most useful" appears in variants A and G; line 19: "ever" is omitted in variants A and G; line 23: "never" appears in A and G.</note>

<summary>Giordano Bruno argues that the order of logical terms in the Lullian system matters because changing the sequence changes which concept acts as the subject and which acts as a descriptor. He establishes "eight laws" for traversing these combinations to ensure no logical nuance is missed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giordano Bruno’s systematic exploration of the combinations of three fundamental principles: Goodness (*Bonitas*), Greatness (*Magnitudo*), and Duration (*Duratio* or *Durans*). Following the patterns established on page 350, Bruno here continues to permute these terms through different grammatical cases—nominative, genitive, and ablative—to demonstrate how their metaphysical relationship changes when one or more act as the primary substance versus a modifying quality.</meta>

<page-num>351</page-num>
<header>ON THE SCRUTINY OF SPECIES.</header>

The goodness of the greatness of that which lasts, <note>original: *durantis*</note> i.e., of that which endures.
Goodness, a lasting greatness.

# OBSERVATIONS CONCERNING THE LULLIAN LANTERN.
<note>original: "Animadversiones circa Lampadem Lullianam." The "Lantern" refers to the "Great Art" of Ramon Llull (1232–1315), a combinatorial system designed to illuminate all knowledge through the systematic arrangement of basic concepts.</note>

---

->13 March [15]87.<-

At the beginning of this contemplation, it must be noted that the foundation of <margin>5</margin> this art <note>original: "huius artis." Here, Bruno refers to the "Art" of Ramon Llull, a system of logic and mnemonics intended to uncover truth through combinations of concepts.</note> and the greatest part of its effectiveness consists in the order and the manner of proceeding. Therefore, since there are many types of methods, there is one unique method suited to this business; so that it may be distinguished from others, it should be observed that some methods are **divisive**, <margin>10</margin> some are **compositive**, some are **inquisitive**, some are **institutive**, some are **constructive**, and some are **mixed**. <note>original: "divisivae, compositivae, inquisitivae, institutivae, constructivae, mixtae." These represent the standard Aristotelian and Scholastic approaches to logical inquiry and teaching.</note>

The **divisive** method is indeed like the **definitive** method, in which, having established a certain subject or "definable" thing, we proceed first by considering its <term>genus<gloss>The broad category or "family" to which a thing belongs (e.g., "animal" is the genus for "human")</gloss></term>, namely, within whose universality <margin>15</margin> it consists; then we consider the primary differences, and finally the last, closest, and immediate differences, down to the single most specific one. This mode is likened to **cognition**, which proceeds from an indistinct and confused whole toward the parts, just as from the perception of a whole human being one moves toward a resolution into parts, such as the head, hands, etc.; <margin>20</margin> and from there to the flesh, bones, etc.; and from there to the four <term>humors<gloss>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed in ancient and Renaissance medicine to determine health and temperament</gloss></term>; from these to the four <term>elements<gloss>The basic building blocks of the physical world: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</gloss></term>; and finally to matter, which is

---

<meta>This page continues Bruno's classification of logical methods. The previous page (359) ended mid-sentence while describing the "divisive" or "definitive" method, which breaks a concept down into its constituent parts.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...a simple body, and the form which is the soul. <note>original: "anima." In the Aristotelian sense used by Bruno, the "soul" is the organizing principle or "form" that makes a living body what it is.</note> Thus, the definition resolves the name of "man" into the parts of its definition.

The **compositive method** <note>original: "Methodus compositiva."</note> is like the order of demonstration; for when it has been proposed whether a <term>property<gloss>original: "passio." In logic, a characteristic or attribute that flows from the essence of a subject (e.g., "the ability to laugh" is a property of humans).</gloss></term> predicated of some subject is stated, that method—having taken up the intermediate terms—by running through them in many ways, joins the predicate with the subject or distinguishes it within the subject.

<margin>58^v</margin>
The **inquisitive method**, which is the same as the **inventive** <note>original: "inventiva," from "invenire," meaning to find or discover.</note> method, is that which proceeds from parts and principles—namely from particulars and things perceived by the senses, which are the parts and principles of knowledge—toward universals and <term>intelligibles<gloss>original: "intelligibilia." Objects or concepts that can only be grasped by the intellect, rather than the physical senses.</gloss></term>; by this means, through induction and examples, universals are proven, from which science is finally made whole.

The **institutive method** <note>original: "Methodus institutiva." This is the method used for "institution" or instruction.</note> is that which proceeds from universals to particulars, and this is suited for discovery, for completion, and for producing <term>instruction<gloss>original: "doctrina." The process of teaching or the body of knowledge being transmitted.</gloss></term> in others; for in this way, common precepts and universal rules are proposed first, before a progression is made to exceptions and particulars specific to individuals. Otherwise, a frequent repetition of the same thing would occur—as if someone wished to teach the nature of animals and renewed the general concept in every single species, when it would have been more efficient to say first what is common to all, second what is common to some, and third what is specific to individuals.

The **directive method**, which is related to the compositive, is when progression occurs from simpler things and elements to <term>composed things<gloss>original: "elementata." Things made up of or formed from more basic elements.</gloss></term>, just as happens among geometers and arithmeticians, who proceed from knowledge of the point, line, and angle to knowledge of figures, which are integrated and formed from these; and...

<summary>Bruno defines four logical methods: the compositive (demonstration), the inquisitive (induction from senses to intellect), the institutive (efficient teaching from general to specific), and the directive (building complex structures from simple elements like geometry).</summary>
<keywords>compositive method, inquisitive method, institutive method, directive method, logic, universals, induction, pedagogy, geometry</keywords>

### REMARKS ON THE LULLIAN TORCH
46

This final mode is easily mixed with certain others, such as the directive mode or the <term>institutive mode<gloss>original: "modo institutivo." A method used for teaching or establishing the foundations of a subject.</gloss></term>. The present art is regulated especially according to this mode; for it proceeds from simple things and the elements of teaching and writing to the most immediate composition, and from the immediate to the remote and final. 

<margin>5</margin> Just as this order of proceeding is proportioned to the order of the grammarians; for just as grammarians have their own alphabet <margin>59^r</margin> containing very few elements, from which infinite words are formed, so this art receives certain simple terms, <margin>10</margin> from which infinite <term>propositions<gloss>Statements that affirm or deny something about a subject.</gloss></term>, enunciations, and definitions are formed, and from which infinite <term>middle terms<gloss>original: "media." In logic, the middle term is the concept that links the subject and predicate in a syllogism.</gloss></term> of arguments are drawn—although there can be a large, but not countless, supply of the most select middle terms. For there do not exist as many middle terms by which we <term>demonstrate<gloss>To prove something with scientific certainty.</gloss></term> <margin>15</margin> as there can be middle terms by which we persuade; nor can those by which we demonstrate seriously and persuade equal the number of those by which we can persuade and demonstrate lightly. 

To these simple elements—which are formed by a triple alphabet (each of which consists of nine elements <note>original: "novem constant elementis." This refers to Ramon Lull’s "Great Art," which used sets of nine concepts (represented by letters B through K) to categorize the attributes of God, relations, and questions.</note>)—there follows, <margin>20</margin> as will be seen, the combination of two elements of a word for the formation of "syllables." This is proportioned to the first operation of the intellect, which is followed by <term>discourse<gloss>original: "discursus." The process of reasoning from one judgment to another.</gloss></term>, which will be seen to consist in the combination of three elements, just as every argumentation, of whatever sort it may be, <margin>25</margin> adopts neither more nor fewer than three terms <note>Every valid syllogism requires exactly three terms: the major, the minor, and the middle.</note>.

**Principles** extend themselves to more things than **causes** (God is a cause, but not a principle <note>original: "Deus est caussa, sed non principium." Bruno is likely distinguishing between a "Cause" as an external agent and a "Principle" as an internal constituent of a thing's nature, though this distinction varied among Renaissance philosophers.</note>), and they are even more general than **elements**. "Elements" are said to be those things which are parts...

### CHAPTER 4.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding the fourth chapter, it should be noted that Ramon Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher who created a "Great Art" (Ars Magna), a logical system intended to prove truths through the combination of basic concepts.</note> reduces all things about which anything can be said to **nine subjects** <term>subjects<gloss>In Llull's system, these are categories of being—God, Angel, Heaven, Man, Imaginative, Sensitive, Vegetative, Elementative, and Instrumentative—intended to cover all of existence.</gloss></term>. These are <term>universals<gloss>General concepts or categories that apply to many individual things.</gloss></term> which, whatever their nature may be, come together for consideration so that something may be either denied or affirmed regarding them. Or, they are considered in such a way as to <margin>10</margin> belong to one or more of these subjects. And certainly, there can be nothing that escapes the logic of these subjects; everything, I say, must be shaped, formed, and enriched according to the <term>likeness<insert>likeness must not</insert></term> <note>original: "similitudinem non." The translator suggests this addition to clarify that nothing can exist without conforming to these logical categories.</note> of one or more of them. Thus, all **expressible things** and all **proposable things** are reduced to these nine, and nothing outside of these nine can be <margin>15</margin> imagined. This is true because even **fictions**—which are the tools of the imaginer, the deceiver, and the one in error—are reduced to their own proper genus. Therefore, the first thing that must be made clear in this art is the reasoning by which any given proposition is referred to its specific class. Following this consideration, we must provide <margin>20</margin> **definitions** for each of these nine. These definitions are so specific to the genera themselves or the underlying qualities that they can be countable and common, or specialized and applied to individuals, universals, and particulars. They apply to everything reducible to them, as they are soon derived through the principles and <margin>25</margin> elements of this art, which are regulated according to that specific logic.

### REGARDING THE FOURTH AND FIFTH CHAPTERS.

<margin>60r</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Once everything has been explained, it must be remembered that although all things that can be spoken of or considered are subjects—insofar as they are submitted to demonstration and consideration—and all things, for one reason or another, can be predicates, as is explained in the text; there are nonetheless certain things enumerated which, by their nature, take on the nature of a subject, while others take on the nature of a predicate. In <unclear>this way</unclear> <note>original: "in qᵃ." Likely a contraction for "in qua" (in which) or "in quibus" (in which things).</note> and to introduce the form of the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the *Ars Magna* of Ramon Llull, a system of logic using letter combinations to explore all possible truths.</note>, it is necessary for all things to be defined and returned to their proper orbit. Now, because for the use of the present Art these things must not only be held in memory, but must also be ready at hand—as the swiftest execution of concepts and arguments is required from one who practices the Art—we have therefore established this brief method <note>Bruno is here providing a "memory palace" or mnemonic shortcut to help the student internalize Llull's complex system.</note>, by which anyone can very quickly grasp what is sought. For one must have ready at hand the **alphabet** <term>alphabet<gloss>In Lullian logic, the letters B through K represent specific sets of principles, such as Goodness, Greatness, Power, and Wisdom.</gloss></term> and the wheel of the nine absolute predicates, the relative predicates, and the wheel of questions. These questions are four in number, each consisting of nine terms signified by the same nine letters. You should choose four groups of people there, so that you have nine known old men, nine known boys, nine known handmaidens, and nine known animals or people of another kind, such as friends, etc. And let their names be (or be imagined to be) such that they have, in order, the first letter corresponding to each of these nine elements, for instance: for **B** you have Barnabas, for **C** Caesar, for **D** Davus, for **E** Eugenius, for **F** Fabius, for **G** William <note>original: "Guielhelmum."</note>, for **H** Honoratus, for **I** John, and for **K** Charles.

E. Regarding the movers of the heavens or the soul of the world <note>original: *anima mundi*, the animating principle of the universe.</note> and the spheres,

The preceding statement is manifest from the fact that, by definition, everything incorruptible is uncreatable.

<margin>10</margin> F. There is neither reason nor sense that can assign a beginning to the motion and growth <note>original: *vegetationi*, referring to the life-force or organic development of the cosmos.</note> of the universe, because in those things which exist, the movable object exists before the motion—since nothing is moved unless it is capable of being moved—and motion exists before the generation of the movable object, because nothing is generated unless it is brought from potentiality into actuality.

<margin>15</margin> G. In the world, there is a desire and a drive toward being forever; indeed, all material things naturally desire to be preserved in existence instinctively <note>original: *inconsulto*, meaning without conscious deliberation or "unconsulted."</note>. If this desire is frustrated in a particular individual, | it must not be frustrated in universal nature, in **61v** which the most excellent motion is found.

<margin>20</margin> H. It is within the power of the nature of the world that it can perpetually move its body, because nothing is contrary to the soul of the world, since she is the "form to be formed" <note>Bruno suggests the world soul is the ultimate organizing principle that shapes all matter.</note>. Now, everything that is destroyed is hindered; although hindrance and corruption may happen to particular things because of their opposing natures, 
<margin>25</margin> the same cannot happen to the universe, even though its constituent parts are opposites.

I. It is better to be than not to be. So also it is better to have existed than not to have existed, and better to exist in the future than not to; for such must be that which is true and good, and

# GIORDANO BRUNO'S OBSERVATIONS ON THE LULLIAN LAMP

K. The end and perfection of every operation is consistency and being; therefore, the universal consistency of the universal work [must exist]; it is necessary that this extends itself to all time. Therefore, it is eternal.

<margin>5</margin>
B. C. <note>In the Lullian system, letters represent fundamental principles. 'B' usually represents Goodness. Here, Bruno combines Goodness with other attributes (C, D, E, etc.) to define the universe.</note> A particular good can exist in a part; but the universal good, which is the same as the greatest good, must exist in the whole. Therefore, the whole creates duration.

B. D. That which is good ought to exist; the universe is good and the greatest good, and it is that which contains all things and toward <margin>10</margin> which all things that are limited reach their end, while it itself has no further point at which it is terminated; therefore, it is the end <note>original: *finis*, meaning the goal or ultimate purpose of existence.</note> and not something that is finished <note>original: *finitum*, meaning bounded or limited.</note>.

<margin>62r</margin>
B. E. The goodness of the world is so great that it can preserve itself, because its power is not limited by anything else, <margin>15</margin> nor does it have an opposite—not only one that might conquer it, but not even one that might resist it; therefore, it possesses absolute and singular power.

B. F. The goodness of the world cannot be understood or comprehended as being corruptible; therefore, it should not be described as such. <margin>20</margin>

B. G. Goodness possesses that which is good; since the world is perfectly good, it possesses perfect goodness; however, this would not be the case if it were likened to a straight line rather than a circular one <note>Bruno follows the classical idea that circularity represents perfection and eternity (having no beginning or end), whereas a straight line represents a finite, linear progression.</note>.

B. H. The goodness of the world is always at the same level of vigor; <margin>25</margin> for it flourishes now in the same way it is seen to have always flourished, as is evident from the fact that the number of species does not increase, even though they vary and change; how much more should such power be attributed to the universe, which restores and contains all things. * * *
